items.body: Listening to Crude Walnut Taste, it is tempting to focus on Giorgi Koberidze‘s compositional rigour: the electroacoustic transformations, the dialogue with Western classical forms, the microscopic attention paid to the behaviour of sound. Those elements are certainly there, but they risk obscuring something equally important. This is a remarkably funny album. After all, the opening track, “Horsing Around”, gives the game away immediately. Crude Walnut Taste is not funny in the sense of parody or quotation, but in the pleasure it takes in constantly wrong-footing the listener who might be expecting an academic work. A gesture suddenly changes direction, a rhythmic idea gathers momentum before being interrupted by an entirely different line of thought. Titles such as “Quasi Sonata-Allegro”, “Experimental, electro-accoustic, spatial audio, Georgian, sound design, Tbilisi, ambient – Adagio” and “Tbilisian Faux-Valse” gesture towards familiar classical forms, but only long enough for Koberidze to dismantle them. As the composer explains in the accompanying interview, these references belong to an earlier period of his practice, when his relationship with classical composition was more direct and, in his own words, more “primitive”. And this is the paradox at the heart of the album. On the one hand it sounds almost primitive, built from raw acoustic matter; on the other, the speed with which ideas appear, collide and disappear constantly propels it forward. Without resorting to the tired label of “retro-futurism”, the image that kept returning while I listened was Georgiy Daneliya’s Kin-dza-dza!. The 1986 Soviet science-fiction comedy follows two ordinary citizens transported to a distant galaxy where advanced civilisation appears to have regressed into something primitive. The film was, of course, scored by the late Georgian composer Giya Kancheli, yet there is a comparable measure of irony and lightness of touch running through both works. That playfulness extends to the sound world itself. Much of the album is constructed from recordings of the doli, the Georgian drum, chosen precisely because it carries no melodic baggage. Rather than treating the instrument as a symbol of national identity, Koberidze breaks it down into tiny fragments that become the raw material for an unexpectedly broad range of textures. The result is music that remains unmistakably physical. Even the electronics rarely transform those sounds outright. However, what remains most surprising, is the album’s speed, and not just its manic kinetic energy, but also the speed with which ideas appear only to mutate. Very little is allowed to settle. Musical thoughts collide with a kind of controlled frenzy that recalls someone thinking faster than they can speak. And yet, despite this restless surface, the music never feels erratic. It remains playful without becoming flippant, rigorous without turning solemn. That is a rare balance, and one that gives Crude Walnut Taste its distinctive character. To help us crack the walnut, we approached Giorgi Koberidze directly. Crude Walnut Taste began life as a 20-channel spatial work commissioned for MONOM’s 4D Sound system before being reimagined in stereo for this release. How did the process of translating such a physically immersive piece into a two-channel format affect your relationship to the material? Were there aspects of the original spatial architecture that had to be sacrificed, or did the reduction reveal new details that were previously hidden? I actually already knew how the piece would sound in stereo, because I don’t have a twenty-channel speaker setup at my studio. So while working on it, I was composing in stereo from the start, imagining what sound could fit where. We then spent two weeks at MONOM Studio in Berlin, where we had the chance to rearrange the piece, add things, and sometimes exclude things, but the core idea of the music was already written in stereo, and that’s what made it possible to translate the twenty-channel piece back down. Of course, a lot is lost in that reduction, but the core idea is still there. It works almost the same as watching an IMAX film in a normal movie theatre: whatever really matters stays in focus, stays at the centre. What the IMAX size gives you additionally is maybe more air, more space, something that isn’t crucial to understanding the film itself. I’d say it’s the same with this piece: what really matters is still there in stereo. The MONOM system just gives more space and some additional ideas, but I wouldn’t say the piece is focused only on those twenty channels. Generally, my belief is that good music can be played on a single-string guitar, even if it was written for a hundred-channel system, as long as the idea itself is strong, and as long as the music matters more than the form. If we’re not talking about a piece where form is more important than the music, then I think it’s easily translatable anywhere. Across Forests, Tales, Cities, Forests, its Epilogue, and now Crude Walnut Taste, the doli seems to occupy an increasingly central role in your work. On this album, the instrument is extensively sampled, dissected and reconstructed through micro-editing techniques. What drew you to the doli as the primary sonic source, and how did transforming it electronically alter your perception of an instrument so deeply embedded in Georgian musical culture? I use the doli because it has no pitch. My problem with using tonal instruments from the Caucasus – the duduk, say, or the chuniri – is that they come with already-written melodies and harmonies, and I find it very hard to know how to use that material in modern music. At some point I decided I would never touch existing melody or harmony, because it’s already there, it’s already enough. It doesn’t need anything from me, or from anyone, to be transformed. The doli is interesting because you can use it without ever touching a melody or a harmony, it gives you a lot of possibility to take micro-material from it instead. But anyone who understands sound and sound design knows that, basically, you can turn any sound into anything. The instrument you choose is just a source for material, and from there you can go anywhere; it’s really about what physical material you’re comfortable working with. In my case, it’s the doli simply because it’s here – you’re in Georgia, there are dolis everywhere, you can just grab one. Also, the quality of that sound already carries something very familiar to every Georgian. By using it, you’re lightly touching this historical heritage, but it doesn’t give you licence to overuse it – to base your music on something already precious to Georgians and then claim it as your own. Some people use old melodies, traditional melodies especially, and I’m not against using old pop music in modern work. But when it comes to traditional music, it’s more delicate. So even when we do use tonal instruments like the duduk, we’re very careful never to cross into an already-written melody from Georgian folk music. Earlier works such as Forests, Tales, Cities, Forests felt almost cartographic, mapping landscapes, memories and imagined geographies through graphic scores, ensembles and field recordings. Crude Walnut Taste seems more focused on texture, gesture and acoustic matter itself. Do you see this album as a departure from those narrative and spatial concerns, or as another way of exploring the relationship between place, memory and sound? Also, several track titles—”Tbilisian Faux-Valse”, “Quasi Sonata-Allegro”, “Experimental, electro-accoustic, spatial audio, Georgian, sound design, Tbilisi, ambient – Adagio”—appear to reference established musical forms, yet the music itself constantly undermines expectations through fragmentation, electroacoustic processing and playful subversion. To what extent are these titles intended as affectionate dialogues with classical traditions, and how important is humour or irony within your compositional practice? First, some context: Crude Walnut Taste was actually written much earlier than Forests, Tales, Cities, Forests – about five years earlier. What the two albums share is a certain playfulness with, and closeness to, classical music. In 2019, when I wrote Crude Walnut Taste, I was a much younger student of classical composition, so the way I integrated that knowledge into the album was more direct, less hidden, even a bit more “primitive” – the melodic and harmonic moments lean more overtly classical. That’s also where the track titles come from, which I actually chose later, closer to the album’s release: names like “Tbilisian Faux-Valse” or “Quasi Sonata-Allegro.” They’re not literal sonata-allegros or waltzes, of course, but the mood and the harmonic gestures really are drawn from there. Looking back, I wouldn’t use these references so directly today – in Forests, Tales, Cities, Forests, similar techniques are used much more hidden, on a deeper, more background level. So, from that perspective, this earlier album carries a bit of irony, a bit of humour, and that’s something I’m quite fond of. I’ve always wanted to find a way to put humour inside music – it’s genuinely hard to do. My friend and musical collaborator Luka, the other half of Awwwaea, always used to come up with wonderfully funny musical ideas; I was constantly amazed at how he could make our whole friend group laugh for hours over a single musical idea. I’d say this album carries a little of that same spirit. At the same time, it’s a very personal record. Even the title comes from childhood: crude walnut taste refers to eating very raw, unripe walnuts as kids – cracking them open with your fingers while they’re still green, watching your fingers turn green and then black from the juice. That taste takes me straight back to those childhood memories: sometimes fast, sometimes a little sad, but mostly very bright, full of colourful images and imagination – but still raw, because the sounds themselves are raw. After I finished the album, a friend told me at a small concert that it felt like “music made for sounds no one else is using.” I loved that description, because the sounds you hear really are raw – almost taken straight from the computer as they are, with very little additional sound design or processing layered on top. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以格鲁吉亚传统鼓doli的原始声音为素材，通过碎片化处理将其转化为丰富的电子声学纹理。作者刻意打破西方古典形式的框架，将奏鸣曲快板、圆舞曲等体裁以解构方式重新呈现，使作品充满出人意料的方向转折与节奏突变。评论指出专辑核心特质在于一种'原始感'与'高速思维'之间的悖论：材料粗糙原始，观念却以极快速度碰撞、变异、消失，形成受控的狂躁。评论将其与苏联科幻喜剧电影《Kin-dza-dza!》的讽刺与轻盈感相比较，强调音乐在严谨学术外表下的游戏性与幽默感。电子处理并未完全转化原始声响，保留了极强的物质性与身体感，呈现出融合格鲁吉亚文化传统与当代实验创作的独特视角。

items.body: 33 takes the traditional age of Christ at his death as the axis of a twelve-part electroacoustic cycle concerned with creation, incarnation, suffering, death and renewal. Yara Mekawei and Amir Rezk draw on biblical passages, Coptic Orthodox liturgy and Arabic recitation, but rarely allow the texts to remain intact: voices are repeated, stretched and submerged until scripture begins to function as rhythm and texture. Dense drones, fractured percussion, recitation and sudden clearings give the record a ceremonial character without turning it into devotional music. Its structure is particularly effective. “LOGOS” begins with John’s “In the beginning was the Word”; by “New Creation,” Revelation has replaced Genesis, with the first heaven and earth passing away and death itself disappearing. Between them, “Mysterion,” “33,” “Harrowing of Hades” and “Sackcloth Love” trace a passage through Eucharist, Crucifixion, descent and mourning. Musically, 33 sits between electroacoustic composition, dark ambient, and industrial electronics with a hint of prog rock, although none of those descriptions quite accounts for its restless construction. Mekawei and Rezk work with low drones, distorted orchestral sonorities, spoken voices, granular processing and percussion that repeatedly breaks apart just as it appears to settle into a pattern. The music can be oppressively dense, then abruptly hollowed out to expose a voice or a thin electronic residue. Rather than using electronics as accompaniment to the religious texts, the pair subject voice and instrumental material to the same processes: syllables become pulses, recitation turns into noise, and acoustic sounds lose their identifiable origins. This constant movement between intelligibility and abstraction gives the album much of its tension. What begins with a private anxiety surrounding the age of 33 expands into a work about mortality and transformation, with ancient texts treated not as historical artefacts but as material that can still be sounded, fractured and inhabited. To help us further navigate the album, we reached out directly to Yara Mekawei and Amir Rezk. 33 seems to follow an unusually coherent spiritual trajectory: from the Logos and creation in “LOGOS” and “Genesis,” through embodiment, suffering and death, to resurrection and finally the New Jerusalem in “New Creation.” Yet the album never feels like a straightforward retelling of scripture; texts are fragmented, repeated, obscured and absorbed into the electronics. Did you conceive the twelve tracks as a narrative or liturgical cycle from the outset, and how important was it that this progression could be felt without necessarily being understood literally? From the very beginning, we did not set out to create a straightforward textual retelling or a literal recitation of scripture. For us, the sacred texts are not static history; they are a living, sonic score. The progression across the twelve tracks was essential because we recognized that the trajectory of Christ’s life, from incarnation and embodiment, through suffering, descent, and ultimate renewal, is not merely a historical or theological timeline. It is a universal, spiritual archetype. It is a pattern that exists in the world and plays out in our own lives, in human endurance, migration, grief, and rebirth, whether we consciously recognize it or not. By weaving Yara’s personal story, her family inheritance, her grandmother’s warning, her lived experience of displacement and transformation, into this grander framework, the album becomes a dual narrative. The fragmentation, repetition, and electronic processing of the texts reflect how personal memory and sacred history actually operate in human consciousness: rarely as a clean, linear text, but as lingering textures, echoes, and internal pictures. It was crucial that a listener could feel this emotional and spiritual weight instinctively without needing to decipher every word literally, because the underlying trajectory of endurance and transformation is something universally felt in the human spirit. The number 33 begins from something intensely personal — a maternal warning about the thirty-third year of life — but the album gradually connects that age to Christ’s suffering, death and resurrection. In the title track especially, the language of Isaiah’s suffering servant and the Crucifixion seems to make personal vulnerability and sacred history overlap. How did that private association with the age of 33 become the organising principle of the record, and did making the album change what that number meant to you? The connection became obvious the moment we realized that 33 was not just a personal chronological marker, but the darkest point in Christ’s earthly life, the threshold of Gethsemane and the Cross, where He faced an unrepeatable cup of unknown suffering and abandonment. In our own human lives, those rock-bottom moments, where we carry an unbearable personal weight or face severe displacement, often become the precise pivots for profound transformation. The warning Yara inherited about the thirty-third year was essentially pointing toward this exact kind of personal Gethsemane: a room where you are tested to your limits, forcing a parallel between our lived vulnerability and what Christ endured. Creating 33 completely changed what that number means to us. Through the process of writing and immersing ourselves in these detailed sonic patterns and raw emotions, 33 transformed from an ominous, looming warning into a symbol of profound solidarity. It fixed a truth in our minds: our suffering in this life is never meaningless, nor is it carried in isolation. The Divine chose to step into human history and share directly in our exact grief, exile, and pain. Through making this record, the thirty-third year ceased to be a room of fear, becoming instead a reminder that we are never truly alone in the dark. Sacred language in 33 occupies a strange position between meaning and sound. Biblical passages, Coptic Orthodox material, Arabic and other vocal fragments can initially be intelligible, but repetition and electronic processing often push them toward rhythm, texture or something resembling incantation. Yara, your previous work has already explored ways of translating sacred texts into sonic structures; how did the two of you approach the voice here? Were you interested in preserving the theological meaning of these texts, or in reaching a point where the sound of devotion itself becomes the compositional material? For us, it was never a choice between preserving theological meaning or turning the text into pure abstraction, we wanted both. We approached the sacred texts as both a coherent narrative framework and a stream of subconscious thought, treating the voice as a primary musical texture. We deeply respect the inherent power of music to imprint a specific fingerprint upon the mind and the soul. However, we wouldn’t use the word “incantation” to describe this process. Instead, we see the voice and its electronic transformations as a sonic blessing carried through the physical sound waves themselves. We knew that many people listening across the world wouldn’t understand Arabic or Coptic, but we believed that sound itself can transcend language barriers. By layering, repeating, and processing these sacred fragments, we wanted to carry the spiritual energy and raw devotion directly to the listener’s intuition. The theological meaning grounds the structure, while the sonic vibration allows the blessing to reach anyone who listens, regardless of whether they can translate the words. There is a striking circularity between the beginning and end of the album. “LOGOS” opens with John’s “In the beginning was the Word,” while “New Creation” ultimately arrives at Revelation’s vision of the first heaven and earth passing away, God wiping away every tear, and death ceasing to exist. Between those points, the music moves through creation, the body, Eucharist, suffering, mourning and resurrection. Do you think of 33 as moving from one creation to another — and, if so, is “new creation” primarily a Christian theological idea for you, or does it also describe a personal process of destruction and transformation that took place while making the record? It is deeply both: a personal process of transformation and a theological truth made manifest. On a personal and artistic level, 33 is our very first collaboration together, so the album itself is literally a “new creation” born from our two individual musical worlds. We share the belief that marrying the arts with the sacred is like bringing heaven and earth together, much like the Incarnation of the Divine Logos coming down to breathe new life into His creation and bloom into a new Tree of Life. J.R.R. Tolkien spoke of artists as “sub-creators” or co-creators alongside the Great Creator. By deliberately inviting the Divine into our sound, making a “new creation” was never about trying to invent a new genre of music; it was about marrying the eternal with the earthly, which makes the work spiritual and new at its core. Making this album was an essential process of bringing light directly into the desolation of our own personal suffering and “stations” of life. It was a way to ground those difficult experiences in hope and meaning, not just for ourselves, but hopefully for anyone who listens to the record. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以基督受难时的33岁为轴心，构建了一个十二乐章的电声循环，涵盖创造、道成肉身、受难、死亡与重生的主题。Mekawei与Rezk运用圣经经文、科普特正教礼文与阿拉伯语诵读，但通过重复、拉伸与淹没的手法使文本脱离原有语境，化作节奏与质感。低频无人机、失真管弦音色、颗粒合成处理与不断碎裂的打击乐交替出现，音乐在极度密集与突然清空之间反复转换，呈现出仪典般的氛围却并非宗教音乐。专辑结构尤为精妙：从《LOGOS》中约翰福音的太初有道，到《New Creation》中启示录的新天新地，中段《Mysterion》《33》《Harrowing of Hades》《Sackcloth Love》依次勾勒圣餐、十字架、下入阴间与哀悼的路径。电子处理并非文本的伴奏，而是与声音素材共同被解构，使音节化为脉冲、诵读转为噪音、声学声响丧失可辨识的来源。这种清晰与抽象之间的持续张力，构成了专辑的核心张力。

items.body: It has been about four years since the Brazilian act Aesthetische released their last full-length album, but in the meantime, Gui Pires and Fab Viscardi have kept us entertained with an annual EP. “Every Beat Matters” serves as a metaphor for everything we can do to fight injustice, fascism, prejudice, war, and more. Musically, this translates into four brand-new tracks followed by three remixes. Aesthetische return to their roots more than ever, recalling their former project, Aghast View, with a sound deeply rooted in EBM. It is a meticulously crafted production boasting rich soundscapes and razor-sharp basslines that once again bring Front Line Assembly to mind. The tracks are driven by stomping beats that give them maximum club appeal. To my ears, the first three tracks all sound like potential singles, although Aesthetische clearly have a soft spot for “Chew The Loop,” which appears in three additional and strong remixes. The vocals round everything out, complemented by well-placed samples. One track remains instrumental, yet sounds incredibly effective. Aesthetische never disappoint, but this new EP is undoubtedly one of their strongest releases to date. It represents intelligent, impactful EBM. (Rating:9). Side-Line reported the release of “Every Beat Matters” on June 26, 2026 via Alfa Matrix. Listen to “Chew The Loop”’: Chew The Loop by Aesthetische About Aesthetische Aesthetische is a Brazilian EBM/industrial duo formed by Gui Pires and Fab Viscardi in 2012. Both musicians were previously known for their work in Aghast View and Biopsy, one of Brazil’s pioneering electro-industrial acts of the 1990s. After Aghast View, the duo launched Aesthetische as a new vehicle for modern EBM fused with trance, techno-body music, and industrial atmospheres. The band signed with Belgian label Alfa Matrix in 2012 and has since maintained an exclusive release partnership with them, issuing a steady discography of albums, EPs, and digital singles across physical and digital formats. Albums “Powerswitch” (2012, Alfa Matrix) – Issued in multiple editions, including a box version. “HybridCore” (2014, Alfa Matrix) – A follow-up blending hard-hitting EBM with more melodic synth textures. “Co3xist3ns3” (2019, Alfa Matrix) – Marked a return after several years, further exploring hybridized EBM and trance. “Rvprty” (2022, Alfa Matrix AM 3400DJ) – A digital-only release containing ten tracks. Singles & EPs “Nachtbrenner” (2013, Alfa Matrix) “Statement / Amplitude Zero” (2013, Alfa Matrix) “Colder Lights EP” (2014, Alfa Matrix) “Dirt And Basslines” (2015, Alfa Matrix) “Cold Is Clean” (2015, Alfa Matrix) “We Follow Blindly” (2016, Alfa Matrix) “In My Aurora” (2017, Alfa Matrix) – Featuring Noemi Aurora on vocals. “MMXX” (2020, Alfa Matrix) “Overflow” (2021, Alfa Matrix) “Boiling Over EP” (2023, Alfa Matrix) “Confidence Is Silent” (2024, Alfa Matrix) Split EP “4.4U [2012.11]” (2012, Alfa Matrix) – Digital compilation shared with Metroland, Mentallo & The Fixer, and Daniel B. Prothèse. Alfa Matrix has continued the pace since, following “Boiling Over” (2023) with “Confidence Is Silent” (2024), “Selling Fear” (2025) and now “Every Beat Matters” in 2026.

items.body: Oh how I want to love you Oh how I love to want you Oh how I love to hate you Oh how I hate to love you A persuasive EBM bassline can make almost any terrible proposition sound like it’s worth considering. Charm School’s Desolation makes the most of that weakness, setting a romance of taunts, submission, and calculated cruelty to a groove with suspiciously good manners. The invitation is easy to accept; the lyrics give you every reason to reconsider. The single pairs the Louisville-rooted, Los Angeles-based project with Matia Simovich of INHALT, who wrote the music, while Andrew Sellers, aka Andrew Charm, supplied the vocals and lyrics. It also serves as the lead single from a forthcoming EP that will include the late Steve Albini’s mix of Simulacra, Charm School’s first single. Matia Simovich of INHALT Simovich opens proceedings with a funky synth bassline, setting old-school synth stabs against drums intent on keeping the floor occupied. Metallic synth accents add a peculiar mechanical funk, their hard surfaces catching against the low end’s easy movement. There’s an EBM discipline to the arrangement and an Italo appetite for pleasure, with a trace of darkwave unease making itself comfortable between the two. Every sharp edge has something supple moving around it. Sellers attacks the vocal with a Stooges-era Iggy Pop drawl, mixed with the timbre and cadence of Lou Reed at his most forceful onstage. The compressed vocal sits prominently in the mix, with reverb sending the words ricocheting as though they were bouncing off sheet steel or passing through the blades of an industrial fan. That peculiar treatment gives each phrase a cold metallic afterimage. As the vocal develops, a bubbling synth figure lifts the groove, lending a playful buoyancy to a song whose romantic prospects are deteriorating by the line. The opening verse treats manipulation as a sales pitch, with a lover boasting of their dishonesty while angling to become the sole object of another person’s belief. By the second verse, that desire for control has tipped into a plea for surrender, even deception, as though being consumed by someone might offer its own peculiar relief. The roles seem to trade places, with domination and dependence feeding the same appetite. Images of kneeling, worship, and bodily sacrifice push the devotion toward something frighteningly absolute. The repeated title leaves that exchange with a bleak destination, while the closing permutations of wanting, loving, and hating keep rearranging the terms without resolving them. Each small change shifts the emotional balance. Pleasure survives in the music even as the words describe a relationship consuming itself, and the bassline keeps making its persuasive case for staying another few minutes. The collaboration also extends a connection dating back to our 2023 coverage of Simulacra, which credited Simovich with drum programming and noted alternate mixes by both Simovich and Albini. The forthcoming EP brings Albini’s version into the release plans alongside this new material, linking Charm School’s first statement to their latest electronic excursion. Listen to Desolation below and order the single here. Desolation by Charm School Sellers formed Charm School with longtime collaborators Matt Filip and Drew English, drawing on a Louisville upbringing steeped in Slint, Crain, and Rodan, alongside the catalogs of Touch & Go and Drag City. The disruptive instincts of PiL, Swell Maps, and The Fall sit beside an affection for Fugazi and Nation of Ulysses. Their debut EP, Finite Jest, appeared in July 2023, followed by the broader musical reach and acerbic satire of January 2025’s Debt Forever. This February’s Schadenfreude Ploy continued their examination of manipulation, tech wealth, and artificial intelligence. On Desolation, that interest in power finds an intimate setting, with two people apparently quite prepared to make each other miserable. Charm School will join Dildox for dates in Louisville and Knoxville before returning to Los Angeles for Oblivion in October. items._cn_summary: Charm School与INHALT成员Matia Simovich合作的单曲《Desolation》以EBM低音线为骨架，融合Italo disco的愉悦律动与暗潮的不安氛围。Simovich编写音乐，Andrew Sellers（Andrew Charm）负责演唱与歌词，声音处理上借鉴Iggy Pop的懒散腔调与Lou Reed的舞台压迫感，混音中加入金属质感的混响尾音，营造出工业冷感。歌词层面，作品围绕欲望、操控与自我欺骗展开，从推销式表白逐步滑向乞求式的臣服，崇拜与献祭的意象将亲密关系推向极端。重复的标题词与不断重组的"想要/爱/恨"句式拒绝给出情感终点，使歌词与音乐之间形成持续的撕裂感。低音线持续提供挽留的律动，而词句则不断瓦解听者停留的理由。作品延续了双方自2023年《Simulacra》以来的合作脉络，并收录了已故制作人Steve Albini的混音版本。

By 1984’s Shout, however, their absurdism had become so synthetically swollen that Puppet Boy could almost pass for another piece of mutant pop comedy. items.body: There was always something faintly threatening about DEVO, even when they were dressed like escaped laboratory technicians and making middle America wonder whether Akron had been contaminated by industrial runoff. By 1984’s Shout, however, their absurdism had become so synthetically swollen that Puppet Boy could almost pass for another piece of mutant pop comedy. DEVO also have a long history of unconventional covers, from the classic Stones track I Can’t Get No Satisfaction, to Jimi Hendrix’s R U Experienced? Bex Delgado, recording as The Phantom Eyes, turns the tables on the Spud Boys: she hears the threat lurking inside Mark Mothersbaugh’s words and gives it a set of fangs. This version of Puppet Boy takes DEVO’s original premise and drags it into the bedroom of an especially disreputable vampire. The synthesizers feel colder and more severe, the rhythm carries a steady club-floor compulsion, and Delgado sings with the cool authority of somebody who already knows which end of the leash belongs in her hand. Mothersbaugh’s lyrics suddenly acquire an uncomfortable erotic logic. Obedience, dependency, affection, and ownership begin rubbing against one another until nobody seems especially interested in establishing boundaries. That change suits The Phantom Eyes remarkably well. Delgado approaches post-punk and dark electronic music through horror, where desire frequently comes with unfortunate contractual obligations and love can involve surrendering both your better judgment and access to daylight. There is humor inside it, too. Any cover of “Puppet Boy” that treats the title with complete solemnity would miss part of DEVO’s genetic code. Delgado preserves the perversity while turning the joke several degrees darker. The accompanying video makes the implication explicit. Filmed by Tori Kellogg/GR4VES in a single evening, it pairs Delgado’s scarlet entity with Sett’s Puppet Boy, a willing captive whose submission appears to have become his natural state. Red satin, CRT distortion, VHS degradation, and physical closeness give the footage the grubby glamour of an 80s vampire cassette discovered behind the counter of a video store that probably should have been investigated by local authorities. Some sequences were even filmed directly from Gr4ves’ CRT, giving the images their wonderfully diseased television texture. “I was trying to embody the spirit of not exactly a dom/sub relationship, but more like a master/servant one,” says Delgado. “This story isn’t romantic in nature, but still has that sweet feeling that the characters do take care of each other. I wanted the Puppet Boy to be not just a “sub,” but rather someone who just doesn’t really know anything else because it’s his whole life–and he has long been fine with this.” The Puppet Boy has no great awakening coming. He knows his place, perhaps enjoys it, and The Phantom Eyes leave him exactly where DEVO put him forty-two years ago: attached to invisible strings, smiling nervously, waiting for somebody else to pull. items._cn_summary: 本文评论了西雅图艺术家Bex Delgado以The Phantom Eyes名义翻唱DEVO 1984年作品《Puppet Boy》的单曲及其MV。评论者认为Delgado的版本发掘了原作中潜伏的威胁感，将其拖入一间声名狼藉的吸血鬼卧室：合成器更加冷峻严苛，节奏拥有舞池般的持续推动力，人声则带着掌控者的冷静权威。Mothersbaugh的歌词在翻唱中展现出令人不安的情色逻辑，顺从、依赖、情感与所有权彼此摩擦，边界消失。Delgado以恐怖视角切入后朋克与暗电子领域，欲望常伴随契约条款，爱意味着交出判断力与日光。MV由Tori Kellogg/GR4VES在一夜之间拍摄，红丝缎、CRT失真与VHS劣化质感营造出八十年代地下吸血鬼录像带的污浊魅力。Delgado本人阐释其主仆关系的主题，强调角色并非浪漫但彼此照看，奴仆早已安于其位。

items.body: Like many others, my gateway into the Coltrane universe was the inevitable Blue Train , a 1997 CD reissue, with the cover altered with different tones from the original edition. I was beginning to discover jazz and, beyond the variations on the title track, it was the vertigo of “Moment’s Notice” that must have won me over at that early stage. And, of course, the free sound of the saxophone, and the fascinating process of its discourse construction in real time — fascinating for someone who, until then, knew nothing of any form of improvised music. From there, there were several landmark records, in a process that did not follow chronology: it went through the duet with Johnny Hartman, Live at Village Vanguard , the space journey of Meditations , all the way to the devotional magic of A Love Supreme , reading the booklet while following the music, and the pinnacle of Ascension . Along the way, an unavoidable landmark, Giant Steps (as with Ornette’s records, the title also announced the jazz that was coming) with its timeless title track and the melancholic sweetness of “Naima”. I was discovering the albums in no particular order, finding the records or having them find me in a random way, and then gradually organizing Coltrane’s journey in my head, as if piecing a puzzle together. In that process, my favorite album then remains my favorite to this day: My Favorite Things . Too mainstream, too easy, some might say. On ’Trane’s path, a milestone. Not yet the classic quartet, but almost there: McCoy Tyner on piano, Elvin Jones on drums, Steve Davis on bass (Jimmy Garrison would join shortly afterwards). Coltrane takes up the soprano saxophone and transforms a well-known popular melody into a piece of his own; starting from the original melody, he transforms it through a profound process of unfurling. From this point on, it would become one of his signature tunes, evolving into other, much more advanced and deconstructed versions. But this is the start. The LP setlist also has three songs that touch the soul of anyone who loves the history of jazz: one by Cole Porter, “Ev’ry Time We Say Goodbye”, and two by the Gershwins: “Summertime” and “But Not for Me”. In the context of Coltrane's quest and discography, My Favorite Things is a turning point. And, in my own listener's journey, it's music that affects me deeply. Nuno Catarino is editorial coordinator of jazz.pt since 2022. He contributes to the national newspaper Público, where he has written since 2007. He is the author, with Márcia Lessa, of the book Improvisando (2019). Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: For this release on Canadian label caduc, Ryoko Akama, Cristián Alvear, Cyril Bondi, and d’incise perform Taku Sugimoto’s “mada”. The first section features pin-pricks of guitar punctuating controlled feedback, harmonium, and bowed metals, each instrument following its own line of single tones, but each modifying perceptions of the pitch, speed, and duration of all the others. Everything moves slowly, quietly. You have to slow down to catch these perceptions — slow down your thoughts, your heart rate, your expectations. Sometimes the tones may disappear completely, due to their own low volume, the masking of other noises in the environs, or your own mind racing ahead and losing the thread. You get the impression that’s ok though. The second section is five minutes of silence, while the third and final one picks up where the first left off, introducing piano and percussion in the place of harmonium and bowed metals. The slowly changing combinations of tones and timbres could be compared to a kind of topology: contours rising and falling in pitch and volume, creating undulating slopes, sharp peaks, and flat valleys of silence. To say that the sounds occur at random is like saying a landscape rises and falls at random. It may well appear that way to you given that you didn’t see the millennia of water and wind erosion that gave rise to the topology now before you; yet some sense of logic is still dimly intuitable, a logic that any geologist would be able to explain. ‘Mada’ means ‘still’ in Sugimoto’s native Japanese, and the stillness of the piece contributes to the landscape-like nature of each section. The performance recorded by Akama, Alvear, Bondi, and d’incise is entrancing, with well-chosen sounds combined with precise control and subtlety. Their deep understanding of the music and of each other’s playing makes what could have been a dull, shapeless exercise into an absorbing panorama of sound. In today’s compulsively frenetic and cacophonous world, stillness is as rebellious and counter-cultural as it is rare; the still contours of music such as “mada” reveal the flatness of everything else.     Taku Sugimoto Ryoko Akama Cristián Alvear Cyril Bondi d’incise caduc
items._genre: experimental / avant-garde / contemporary classical / drone / improvisation
items._cn_summary: 这是一张由多位音乐家合作演绎杉本拓作品'まだ'的专辑，发行于加拿大小厂牌caduc。作品分为三个段落，以极低音量、缓慢速度展开，由吉他拨弦、受控反馈、风琴、弓拉金属物等单音构成，音高、速度与时值相互影响彼此感知。第二段为五分钟完全静默，第三段引入钢琴与打击乐器取代风琴与弓弦金属。作者以'拓扑学'类比音色的高低起伏与静默低谷，暗示作品结构并非随机而是经过漫长雕琢的地貌。杉本拓以日语'まだ'（意为'仍然/静止'）命名此作，在当今喧嚣世界中凸显静止的反叛性。演绎者展现出对彼此演奏的深层理解与精确控制，使作品成为一片引人沉浸的声音全景。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由内罗毕新厂牌Cool Waters发行，是德国出生的肯尼亚驻地打击乐手Sven Kacirek与83岁传统肯尼亚歌手Ogoya Nengo及Olith Ratengo的三重奏合作。Nengo来自肯尼亚东部，带来深厚的dodo传统歌唱底蕴，而Ratengo与她比邻而居、共享音乐根源，两人声部相互抛接。Kacirek以Buchla合成器、手打击乐与套鼓构建声音基底，层层叠加的合成多节奏以近乎隐形的方式浮现，使合成器与人声从最初的僵硬并置逐渐化为有机整体。专辑展示了非洲传统与电子实验之间真正的跨文化对话，根源成为前卫，创新看似古老，将不同文化语境编织进21世纪的声响之中。

items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. items._cn_summary: Dorothy Moskowitz联合前卫作曲家与诗人合作的专辑《Songs of Compassion》收录十一首歌曲，以钢琴为核心铺陈，配合弦乐、木管与合成器声场，呈现出非线性的声音结构。评论将其类比为Steve Reich与Philip Glass，旋律不以传统功能和声推进，而是随意识流起伏，强调每个歌词的价值。Moskowitz的人声如同资深方法派演员，对抗威权的政治性歌词延续1960年代抗议传统，同时亦有对死亡与宇宙位置的沉思。专辑试图挑战听众对西方和声运动的固有认知，召唤更古老、更遥远的另类音乐叙事。独立厂牌Silentes发行，整体呈现出将诗歌、政治与现代作曲融合的独特艺术视角。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — Terrifying Angels by Pure Reason Revolution sees the band making their darkest and heaviest album to date, but still keeping specific musical quirks that the band are known for. Taking their new prog sound into elements that include dark ambient, nu metal, psychedelic, symphonic and alternative rock, it proves that Jon Courtney's project still has heavy weight and impression. The trade off of vocals between Courtney & Annicke Shireen are mixed perfectly, with great depth and tone, while musically the band explore all aspects of their sound, making this a true stand out in their discography. While the longer tracks are the true attention grabbers, the shorter songs do keep to their more classic sound with heavier elements. I'd give this a low to mid 8 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is Terrifying Angels.

items.body: Then Comes Silence have reached a point where the more interesting question is no longer whether they have an identifiable sound, but what they are prepared to do with an identity that has become so clearly their own. Formed in Stockholm in 2012 and operating since 2022 as the trio of Alex Svenson, Hugo Zombie and Jonas Fransson, the band are now approaching their eighth album, “Requiem Ballroom,” due on 20 November 2026 via Metropolis Records. Conceived as a diptych, the record divides itself between Requiem and Ballroom, darkness and light, while recent singles “Judgement Day” and “Remaker Redeemer” have already begun to expose the contrast between those two halves. When I spoke with the band in 2024, our conversation touched on originality, conformity and the peculiar conservatism that can develop inside a scene supposedly built around difference. Two years later, those questions have become even more relevant. Rather than discussing “Requiem Ballroom” track by track, we returned to the larger tensions around it: how a band changes without performing reinvention for its own sake, when identity becomes formula, whether nostalgia can disguise itself as tradition, what happens when a trio becomes more focused by becoming smaller, and why sustaining a life in music may now be a harder problem than sustaining an artistic identity. Then Comes Silence interview Karo: When we spoke in 2024, Alex, you said the dark scene develops slowly and needs more originality. Two years later, Then Comes Silence are still immediately recognisable. How do you distinguish a strong identity from a language that has simply become comfortable? Alex: I still think the dark scene is developing very slowly. Can you honestly hear much of a difference between 2019 and 2026? The sound is basically the same, and most of the melodies still follow the same structures. I don’t know what others say about us, but I do think we distinguish ourselves from much of the scene by focusing more on the songs than on the sound. In that sense, we work in a rather traditional way: intro, verse, bridge and chorus. But who am I to judge? If people want to hear the same snare drum, synth pads and chorus-soaked guitars over and over again, maybe that’s what makes them feel good. I just know that we, Then Comes Silence, don’t really think that way. Karo: Your music has never depended on radical stylistic reinvention. Do you think artistic development can happen through changes in proportion, tension and emphasis rather than through introducing obviously new genres or sounds? Hugo: I think it can be a bit of everything you mention. We mix elements of different genres, such as that euro disco synth on “Judgement Day,” and this time we even tried new, exotic instruments in the recording. Both act as new ingredients in the Then Comes Silence sound. But just like a pizza, you can add different toppings and it will still be a pizza. Karo: “Requiem Ballroom” is built around opposites: darkness and light, ending and renewal. Yet Then Comes Silence have often been most interesting in the spaces between opposites: melody and severity, electronics and physical rock instrumentation, melancholy and momentum. Is the album’s binary structure something you actually believe in, or something you wanted to test and complicate? Alex: We believe in everything we do. There’s no theatre. This album is an experiment and a game. Team this vs team that. Karo: The two halves were mixed separately, by Tom van Heesch and Jon Bordon, but still have to exist as one Then Comes Silence record. Where does the identity of the band ultimately reside if the same material can be viewed through two different sonic perspectives? Hugo: The two halves were mixed separately, and recorded differently: different drums, amps, guitars. We wanted them both to have a distinct sound, but at the same time we didn’t want the album to feel like a compilation, so there’s still a sense of coherence between them. The identity of the band is there because it’s the same band using different approaches. Karo: Since becoming a trio, the band has sounded increasingly focused rather than reduced. Has having fewer people in the room actually widened the musical possibilities because the core identity became clearer? Hugo: It’s easier to work with a smaller team of totally focused people than a bigger team that includes distracted people with other priorities. That will only slow you down. Our roles in the band are totally clear; we are all focused on what we are doing, and that allows us to be more effective. Karo: You have now reached your eighth album. At this stage, is reinvention still a useful ambition, or does it become more interesting to understand more precisely what Then Comes Silence should never lose? Alex: We have been constantly active for years and haven’t really taken a break from each other or from music. The soul of Then Comes Silence will always stay the same, no matter how many times we reinvent ourselves. Karo: In our previous conversation, you spoke very positively about the Goth and Post-Punk community but also criticised its tendency towards conformity. Now that Then Comes Silence themselves are an established part of that scene, is it harder to criticise its conventions from the inside? Hugo: We all love the Goth and Post-Punk community. It’s our home. But I don’t think it matters how established you are; conformity will always be the enemy of creativity, which is meant to be at the core of this scene. For me, there are a lot of bands using the same formula, and it feels boring. But then again, others could think that we are doing the same, so in the end it doesn’t really matter. It’s just about what you enjoy listening to and what you don’t. Karo: You also mentioned then that younger audiences in the US gave you hope for the future of the scene. Two years and a great deal of touring later, do you still see a generational difference in how people approach Goth and Post-Punk, or has that picture become more complicated? Hugo: We are starting to notice more youngsters in the audience in Europe too. And that’s amazing. Precisely here in Stockholm we have a really nice and growing scene of young people making music, DJing, going to shows, and that’s great to see. Karo: A band with a long catalogue eventually develops an unwritten contract with its audience: there are sounds, songs and emotional qualities people expect. Do those expectations ever become creatively restrictive, or can they provide a useful resistance to work against? Alex: We’re always prepared to get caked by disappointed fans. We still get comments from people who miss a fourth member to fill the void of a second guitar. Thankfully, we’re in good company. The large majority of our followers are right there with us. Wherever we go, they follow. And wherever they point, we go. Karo: Then Comes Silence have always drawn from older Goth and Post-Punk traditions without sounding like a historical reconstruction. As that original musical history moves further into the past, what makes the difference between inheritance and nostalgia for you? Hugo: I think that we’re definitely not a nostalgia band. We don’t try to sound retro. But we listen to a lot of different genres, and most of the music we listen to is old. I mean, we are not trying to sound like Sisters of Mercy, The Mission or Lords of the New Church, but we probably have the same influences they had back then. Karo: The imagery surrounding “Requiem Ballroom” revolves around symbolic death, transformation and renewal. After more than a decade as a band, does the idea of renewal mean something different now than it would have when Then Comes Silence began in 2012? Alex: No, the only differences would be practical ones. A new instrument, new effects pedals, or a new producer behind the mix. The artistic renewal will always come from within. Karo: Looking beyond this album, what question about Then Comes Silence remains unresolved for you? What are you still trying to understand about this band that eight albums have not answered yet? Alex: Artistically, I have no comments and no expectations about what’s to come. I feel no anxiety about the music, and I don’t really care what other people say. But on the other hand, I’m trying to understand why we can’t make a living from what we do, and why it’s so difficult to reach a wider audience. The inflation affecting everyone on this planet doesn’t seem to apply to artists. People still don’t want to pay more for a show ticket, while they seem willing to pay twice as much for gas, milk or eggs in the store. Touring artists are facing higher and higher expenses, and many of them would probably need to cancel shows just to make ends meet. But they don’t, because there simply aren’t any realistic alternatives for live music. It must be even harder for the new young generation of musicians. I can’t see why it wouldn’t be. I’m trying to understand it, but I still haven’t found a good answer. About Then Comes Silence Then Comes Silence were formed in Stockholm in 2012 by vocalist, bassist and keyboard player Alex Svenson. Drummer Jonas Fransson joined in 2015, followed by guitarist Hugo Zombie in 2018; since 2022, the band have operated as a three-piece. Their discography has moved through labels including Novoton, Nuclear Blast, SPV and Metropolis Records, while extensive touring has taken them across Europe, North America and, in 2026, Latin America. Their eighth studio album, “Requiem Ballroom,” will be released on 20 November 2026 via Metropolis Records. Structured as two contrasting halves, Requiem and Ballroom, the album uses darkness and light not simply as visual motifs but as different approaches to arrangement and production. The current singles are “Judgement Day” and “Remaker Redeemer,” with the latter introducing the Ballroom side and its themes of rebirth, cleansing and beginning again.
items._cn_summary: Then Comes Silence 即将发行第八张专辑《Requiem Ballroom》，专辑以双联画形式构建，对立于安魂与舞厅、黑暗与光明两极。乐队成员在访谈中坦承暗潮场景发展迟缓，多数作品的旋律结构与音色套路多年不变，但他们选择以传统歌曲结构为核心，在编曲配比中寻求变化而非彻底重塑。乐队在新作中尝试引入欧陆迪斯科合成器音色与异域乐器，延续intro-verse-bridge-chorus的框架，但通过不同元素的调配比例来维持辨识度与新鲜感之间的张力。访谈触及了身份与公式之间的模糊地带、怀旧如何伪装为传统、三人编制精简后如何增强聚焦力，以及在音乐场景中维持生计比维持艺术身份更为艰难的现状。

items.body: John Coltrane - Olé (Atlantic, 1961) In the mid-1990s I had just graduated from undergrad with a degree in Journalism and absolutely no idea what to do next. I spent the following summer living in a shared house with five other people about my age, one of whom was a good friend and musical partner in our band called “ Joe Joe the Dog Face Boy. ” We were working, we were playing music, all in all, it was fine even if a bit of a confusing time in life. In the living room of the house, next to my room, was a shelf with a bunch of records on it. The records belonged to my friend, who had just been gifted them by his father. He had placed them on the shelf not knowing what to do with them - I am not sure that he even had a record player at this point, as it was the heyday of CDs afterall. I, however, did have a record player that had been accompanying me all through college and would be my only constant companion for the next twenty years or more, so the records, a rather eclectic mix of music from the 60s and 70s, would end up often on my stereo. This was how I encountered Ol é. Olé , John Coltrane’s last album for the Atlantic label, released in 1961, was recorded with his long-time associates MyCoy Tyner on piano and Elvin Jones on drums, which already likely brings certain harmonic and rhythmic sounds to mind. Joining them was trumpeter Freddie Hubbard, bassists Reggie Workman and Art Davis, and the great Eric Dolphy on flute and alto sax. It was the title track that caught my ear. Extending over the whole side A of the album, it’s a modal feast that builds on a vamp derived from a Spanish folk song. Here, it starts with a single churning bass line and Tyner’s pulsating chords balancing on Jones' driving swing. Soon, Coltrane joins on soprano sax with an approach reminiscent of his playing on ‘My Favorite Things.’ Then, Dolphy lends his flute to the mix, paving the way for Hubbard’s solo, from which the track really takes off. It was rhythmically dense music, but not overly dissonant or harsh; however, for ears that could listen to jazz but were more attuned to rock, it was the perfect hook - a little more advanced than what I was used to, but not too steep of a climb. The B-side’s, ‘Dahomey Dance’ and ‘Aisha’ were a bit more rooted in the ‘jazz’ I knew. I enjoyed them, but it was the A-side that pushed me as a listener. Critics have called Olé a transitional album. Aside from the label change, Coltrane was also headed towards more experimental realms. For me, Olé and that pile of records also came at a transitional time, and helped reveal new paths and possibilities. Thelonious Monk with John Coltrane (Jazzland, 1961) My plan was to next dig into something in that experimental realm. I had my sights on Offering: Live at Temple University, a live album recorded in 1966, shortly before Coltrane passed away, and released posthumously by Resonance Records in 2014. A funny thing happened, however, along the way. As I was pulling up the recording, I passed by Thelonious Monk with John Coltrane and stopped in my tracks. Also released in 1961 on the Jazzland label, this set of evergreen Monk tunes that had been recorded by Coltrane and Monk in '57 and '58 with changing rhythm sections. Two seconds of the opening ‘Ruby, My Dear’ and I knew I’d wanted to spend a little time awith this one again before moving on. As the story goes, Coltrane was addicted to heroin and had just been fired from Miles Davis’ group. He took this break, and cleaned himself up and started to play with Monk. A residency at the Five Spot in NYC in ‘57 is the stuff of legends and a concert recording of the two from 1957 was discovered and released in 2005 by Blue Note, lends credence to the stories. Entitled Thelonious Monk Quartet with John Coltrane at Carnegie Hall, it underscores the copacetic musical relationship found on the original release. Back to that recording: the tune that stopped me in my tracks, the slow moving ‘Ruby, My Dear’ begins with such a melancholic saxophone playing the yearning melody that it instantly romanticizes any space where it’s played. ‘Tinkle, Tinkle,’ with its playful and up-tempo melody gives Coltrane a chance to unfurl those ‘sheets of sound’ that he’s famous for. Similarly on ‘Nutty’, the sheets return in a generously flowing solo, studded at key points with with reminders of the melody. Drum and bass outlining the tune, Monk waiting to come back in with the melody, before abstracting it into Improvisational flurries. This album album is a high point in two musical catalogs that are festooned with them. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评以个人回忆为切入点，回溯了作者在1990年代中期初次接触John Coltrane 1961年专辑《Olé》的经历。乐评详细解析了专辑同名标题曲的结构与编排：从单一贝斯线条和Tyner的和弦铺陈出发，Coltrane以高音萨克斯加入，呼应《My Favorite Things》中的演奏手法，随后Dolphy的长笛与Hubbard的小号独奏层层推进，使乐曲进入更自由的即兴空间。专辑基于西班牙民歌音型构建模态框架，节奏密集却不过分刺耳，被定位为Coltrane从Atlantic转向Impulse时期的重要过渡作品。乐评同时涉及Coltrane与Monk合作的现场录音，展现了对Coltrane从硬波普到自由爵士演变轨迹的关注。整体文笔带有强烈的个人怀旧色彩，将音乐聆听与人生转折期相联系，对Coltrane音乐语言的演变提供了较为深入的分析视角。
