items.body: Strikkland are easy to misread if you mistake humour for distance. Henrik Johansson can deliver brutal lyrics while smiling, appear in a red feather boa, play with national flags or deliberately puncture the visual severity traditionally associated with EBM, but none of that suggests embarrassment about the genre. Quite the opposite. The joke works because the attachment underneath it is genuine. They are not standing outside EBM making fun of its conventions; they know those conventions intimately enough to interfere with them. I first saw the Gothenburg duo at E-Only in 2024 and again this year on the much larger Waldbühne at Nocturnal Culture Night. At NCN, something became particularly clear: humour had stopped feeling like something happening around the songs and had become part of Strikkland’s performance language itself. Hard electronic structures, Henrik’s forceful delivery and the physical directness of EBM remained intact, while gestures, costumes and irony continually destabilised the expectation that seriousness must look solemn. Their second album, “Hommage”, makes that tension especially interesting. It openly acknowledges the music that formed Henrik and Henric, while its production deliberately returns to hardware, physical studio equipment and recording practices associated with an earlier era. Yet Strikkland have little interest in turning EBM into heritage preservation. For them, tradition is useful precisely when it can still be disturbed. We spoke about growing into a band after fifty, refusing genre uniforms, why limitation can generate creativity, the ethics of AI, the strange authority of old symbols, and what happens when two people who take EBM very seriously refuse to behave as though seriousness requires a permanent scowl. Strikkland interview Karo: I first saw you at E-Only in 2024 and then again on the much larger Waldbühne at NCN this year. What struck me at NCN was how much more clearly humour had become part of the performance language itself. When did you realise that humour could be structural to Strikkland rather than merely something happening between songs? Henrik: We have always had humour as an important element of what Strikkland is all about. We started the band on impulse and as a fun thing to do. The lyrics are often conjured up at the same time as we are in the studio creating new songs. My texts often tend to drift towards dark stories about space, death, fantasy and the absurd. The humour you get from seeing the band live is something we have developed throughout all the time we have been on stage. We have fun, and that creates what we deliver. Henric: We realised early on that two old geezers would only look ridiculous if we tried to act tougher or darker than we actually are. Besides, there are plenty of bands already biting heads off chickens or dressing up in full combat gear on stage. It has all been done before, and it really didn’t seem like an option for us. Our appearance and the way we behave also evolved from criticism in Sweden after our first live shows in the early days: “Their music is half-decent, but they aren’t a real EBM band because they don’t look or behave like one.” We kind of turned that against the critics, embraced it even more and made it our thing. Karo: At NCN you told me that when you started the band, already approaching your fifties, you briefly considered becoming the “gothiest” band possible before deciding that pretending to be something you were not would be ridiculous. Did starting Strikkland later in life actually give you a kind of freedom younger bands sometimes lack, because you had less need to prove that you belonged? Henrik: Absolutely! Also, later in life you have so many more musical influences to choose from and try to implement into your own songs. Starting a band later in life also means you can afford to have a band and go places to play live without starving and sleeping in the car on the way there. We are doing something today that you thought impossible when you were young. Henric: Being close to 50 when you start a band certainly provides more freedom. Our ambition was never to release records or perform live, but when possibilities opened up, we jumped for it. Speaking for myself, I got a chance to do what I wanted to do in my teens but never got the chance to do. At 50, you aren’t as afraid of criticism or about what others might think as you are at 16 or 17. That helped a lot. Karo: EBM has accumulated a very strict visual and behavioural vocabulary: severity, discipline, confrontation, often a certain cultivated lack of humour. You clearly love the genre, but you also interfere with those conventions constantly. Which parts of EBM do you take completely seriously, and which parts do you think deserve to be laughed at? Henrik: We never laugh at EBM, but we think we can involve irony and humour in the genre and have a laugh at certain aspects of life. Humour and art are always found in the contrasts. I mostly write quite dark lyrics, but we present them with a lot of smiles, humour and dance. Henric: EBM has been a huge part of my life since the 1980s, so it is something I take very seriously. I do laugh at some of the rigidity coming from certain corners of the fanbase, though. Come on, loosen up and dance while you still can. Have fun. At least laugh a little. There are enough bitter middle-aged men in the world, and I don’t want to become one of them. Karo: That is also why “Hommage” interests me. It is explicitly a tribute to the music that formed you, but homage can easily become imitation. How do you honour an artistic language without treating it as something that should remain frozen in the period when you first discovered it? Henrik: The tribute to the EBM bands we grew up with is always there when we make music. In “Hommage”, it is in the basslines, the sounds, the technology and the artwork. I am a curious person, so I constantly look for new music and new bands to listen to. The EBM genre, and Strikkland, keep finding new ways without letting go of the legacy of the bands of the 80s. Henric: Apart from a handful of gems from bands like Kraftwerk, DAF, Nitzer Ebb, Front 242 and a few others which can’t be topped, EBM and electronic music have evolved a lot. In my playlists there are rarely any songs older than two or three years. You can still hear where it is coming from, but it has evolved. If we stick to what we grew up with, there would be stagnation and the genre would surely die out. But thanks to artists like SIIE, Emmon, Plastikstrom and many others, it is still interesting. So I would rather risk going outside the standard formula and at least try to contribute to keeping EBM alive, both musically and visually. Karo: You made “Hommage” deliberately with classic studio equipment, hardware synthesizers and drum machines, and you were very explicit about not using AI. Is that primarily an ethical position, an aesthetic one, or did you simply want the limitations of those tools to become part of the composition? Henric: AI has no place in art. Full stop. For both creative and ethical reasons. When it comes to using hardware versus working “in the box”, it is purely a workflow decision. The tactility of turning knobs and pushing buttons works better for me than using plugins. We are also privileged enough to get to work together with Hans Olsson at Svenska Grammofonstudion in Gothenburg, which is both a studio and a “synthesizer museum”. It would be stupid not to use all of those classic machines if you can. Our first album, “Bodypop”, was mixed there on an SSL 4000E console, so when we got the chance to mix “Hommage” at Hansa in Berlin on their SSL console, of course we took the plunge. And of course we did some additional recordings there as well. I mean, who could resist playing the very same Steinway grand piano that Martin Gore posed in his jocks next to? Karo: There is an interesting contradiction there: Strikkland describe themselves as expanding the borders of EBM, yet “Hommage” deliberately looks backwards in terms of production practice. Can technological limitation actually be more progressive than unlimited technological possibility? Henrik: Well, maybe in a way every EBM band today is expanding the borders of EBM? To stay in the genre, you have to remain within the frame agreed upon, regardless of what technology you use. But it gets more interesting if you drift away towards the border and sometimes cross it, bringing in other influences and expressions. That’s the way music has always evolved. Henric: For me, limitation sparks creativity. There is a certain number of available channels on a physical mixing console. On a computer, you can have hundreds. There are also limitations to hardware synthesizers and effects, and all of this forces me to be creative. As mentioned before, this is a workflow that suits me. With that said, most of our songs start out “in the box” because it is convenient. Karo: Henric writes the music and programming while Henrik handles vocals and lyrics. With such a clear division, where does the personality of a Strikkland song emerge? Does the music arrive with a character already inside it, or can the vocal idea fundamentally alter what Henric thought he had written? Henrik: Often we start with a bassline that Henric has created and then build it together from that point. I get inspiration for the lyrics and write them at the same time as Henric starts to develop the music. When both of us feel ready, we fuse it all together. This is a fast process, so we are very much in line with what kind of music we want to produce. Henric: Let’s put it this way: when Henrik enters the studio, I might have 20 loops that I have worked on for six months, with basslines, drums and maybe a melody ready. If Henrik says, “Great! But can we change this or that?”, that loop goes into the bin. But if he stops, shuts up and starts to write text immediately, I know it is a keeper. Then we combine that idea into a draft by making a rough arrangement, tweaking the text, tweaking the music and finally recording it. When we have enough tracks for an album, we take it to Hans and re-record everything. So, to answer your question, the music inspires the vocals and the vocals give direction to the final piece of music. Neither would be the same without the other. Karo: At NCN, Henrik changed clothes, exaggerated gestures and played with Swedish and German symbols and declarations of friendship. In a genre that has historically borrowed heavily from militarised imagery, does humour give you a way to use those symbols without allowing them to retain all of their old authority? Henrik: When I go to see a band live, I want to be entertained. When I am on stage, I want to entertain and have a good time! To joke around and interact with the audience and get a warm response elates me. I love the contrast of delivering hard-hitting music and brutal lyrics with a smile on my face and prancing around with a red feather boa. So yes, it is absolutely a way to deflate the power of symbols of power. Henric: Personally, I think it is important to reclaim symbols like national flags from fascists and extremists and use them in a positive way. We don’t hide behind humour and irony, but instead use them as tools for communication. Our message is clear. We don’t accept fascists, Nazis or totalitarian regimes, we support Ukraine’s fight for freedom and we advocate free speech. But maybe we have chosen a “lighter approach” to convey this than other bands, mainly because the darker image doesn’t suit us on a personal level. Karo: What I particularly liked was that none of this reduced the concert to parody because the musical foundation remained genuinely hard. Do you consciously protect that balance, making sure the joke never becomes an excuse for musical weakness? Henrik: When we make our music, we never implement humour to start with. Okay, some lyrics are rather absurd and some sound effects we add for fun, but we want our music to be serious and taken seriously. It is mostly when we play live that we joke around. Henric: Some people have clearly written us off as a parody act. No question about that! But either they haven’t seen us perform live or they haven’t understood what we are doing. Irony is a tough nut to crack for some, and others lack humour. One thing is certain, though. We would never release or perform anything that we ourselves thought was weak, and we put a lot of work into our music. Karo: You worked with Hans Olsson at Svenska Grammofonstudion and Hansa Studios on “Hommage”. Did working in spaces carrying so much recording history make you more conscious of tradition, or was the important thing precisely to forget the mythology once you were actually inside the studio? Henric: It took a while for it to sink in once we were at Hansa. We were actually sitting at the same mixing console that was used to make some of the greatest albums of my youth?! Insane! But once that feeling disappeared, it was just another day in the studio and we did our thing together with Hans. Henrik: Hans Olsson suggested mixing the album at Hansa, and I honestly was totally unaware of the history of this studio. Henric was jumping up and down with excitement. We were there for three days and it finally dawned on me how cool it was! There we could use the same machines and instruments that our heroes used. Karo: The larger stage at NCN seemed to suit you surprisingly well. Some electronic acts compensate for space by simply making every gesture bigger; with Strikkland, the additional room seemed to expose more of the interaction between you. Has playing larger stages changed the way you understand what the visual side of the band can do? Henric: We are not that used to playing larger stages. Apart from Subkultfestivalen in Sweden and WGT, most of our shows prior to NCN have been in front of a maximum of 200 to 300 people. I think there is a lot of room for visual improvement when playing the larger stages. We are just two guys and a couple of machines, so in order to put on even better shows we probably need some additional features on stage to make an impact. But we also don’t want to hide behind video walls, smoke and lasers. Guess it’s time to put on our thinking caps and find a Strikkland solution to the problem. But yeah, visuals are important to us, from album covers to how we appear on stage. Henrik: What Henric said. Karo: “Hommage” looked deliberately towards the music that made you. Looking ahead, what would be the opposite gesture? Is there something in the EBM tradition, perhaps even something you personally love, that Strikkland now need to leave behind in order to find out what the band can become next? Henrik: I can’t think of a thing in the EBM tradition that we want to leave behind. When we create new songs, all kinds of new influences colour the final result. Last time we met, the song rotated towards techno music, so who knows? I always get new ideas every time I listen to metal music. There you find my inspiration and trigger to do new stuff for Strikkland. But with that said, there will never be a guitar on stage with us. Body music forever! Henric: I don’t know, to be honest. There are most certainly no holy cows as far as Strikkland is concerned. What we would love to happen is to do even more shows in mainland Europe, and if that means we will have to tweak things one way or another, so be it. If it turns out we have to bite heads off chickens or perform in Pickelhauben in order to get booked, it might be worth a shot! I mean, a lot of people do judge books by the cover, and it would be sad to miss out because of that. We will see what happens and what we come up with. About Strikkland Strikkland are an electronic body music duo from Gothenburg, Sweden, consisting of Henric Ceder, responsible for music and programming, and Henrik Johansson, responsible for vocals and lyrics. Their first documented release, “Predatorial Right”, appeared on 27 March 2020. Their debut full-length album, “Bodypop”, followed on 2 December 2022. The ten-track record was mixed and mastered by Hans Olsson at Svenska Grammofonstudion in Gothenburg, using an analogue SSL 4000E console; Strikkland explicitly connected that production choice to their admiration for classic EBM. Their second full-length, “Hommage”, was released on 28 March 2025. The nine-track album was produced by Hans Olsson, with recording, mixing and mastering work carried out at Svenska Grammofonstudion in Gothenburg and Hansa Studios in Berlin. The band describe the album as a tribute both to the artists who inspired them and to older recording practices. They state that no AI was used in its production, relying instead primarily on classic studio equipment, hardware synthesizers and drum machines.
items._cn_summary: Strikkland 是来自哥德堡的二人组，他们的第二张专辑《Hommage》明确致敬EBM传统，却拒绝将其变成遗产式的封存。制作刻意回归硬件与早期录音工艺，Henrik 的歌词常涉及太空、死亡、幻想与荒诞，而舞台上的红色羽毛围巾、国旗道具与讽刺姿态则不断消解EBM惯有的严肃视觉。乐评指出，幽默并非掩饰距离感的手段，而是乐队语言本身的一部分——两位年过五十的成员从一开始就意识到假装冷酷只会显得滑稽。他们对类型的掌握足够深入，以至于可以自如地干扰其惯例。专辑在硬核电子结构与反讽表演之间制造张力，既保留了EBM的力量感与直接冲击，又让传统保持被扰动的可能。

items.body: Delerium released the single “Into The Light”, featuring Diamanda Galás, on 23 September 2026 through Metropolis Records. It is the first single from Delerium’s new album “Exaudire”, set for release on 22 January 2027. Into The Light (with Diamanda Galás) by Delerium “Into The Light” incorporates portions of “Deliver Me From Mine Enemies”, written and performed by Diamanda Galás and included on her 1986 album “The Divine Punishment”, the American avant-garde singer’s Mute Records release that opened her “Masque of the Red Death” trilogy. The Delerium track sets that material inside the group’s own production, credited to founding members Bill Leeb and Rhys Fulber. “Exaudire” follows Delerium’s 2023 album “Signs” and carries twelve tracks, continuing the group’s format of pairing largely downtempo, atmospheric songwriting with a rotating cast of guest vocalists: Higher Power (with Mimi Page) Into The Light (with Diamanda Galás) Dream Palace (with Magic Wands) Buried Light (with Mimi Page) Apocalypse (with Inna Walters) Stolen (with Phildel) Into The Unknown (with Jaël) Multiplying Zero (with Inna Walters) Chasing The Wind (with Mimi Page) Exaudire Had To Go (with Jaël) Litany (with Mimi Page) About Delerium Delerium was founded in Vancouver, Canada, in 1987 by Bill Leeb and Rhys Fulber, both already active as members of the electro-industrial group Front Line Assembly. Where Front Line Assembly carried the pair’s aggressive, rhythm-driven material, Delerium became the outlet for their dark ambient and instrumental compositions, released through Dossier and Third Mind before the project moved to Nettwerk for its commercial breakthrough. From the mid-1990s onward, starting around “Semantic Spaces” (1994), Delerium began inviting guest vocalists to front largely downtempo songs on each album, a format the group has kept since. That approach produced its best-known track, “Silence”, featuring Sarah McLachlan, which reached number three in the UK singles chart following a series of 2000 remixes and won two Juno Awards for Best Dance Recording. Delerium music has since appeared in films including “Brokedown Palace” and “Lara Croft: Tomb Raider”, and “Silence” featured more recently in the BBC drama “Industry”. With Front Line Assembly already on the Metropolis Records roster, Delerium signed to the label for the albums “Mythologie” (2016) and “Signs” (2023). “Into The Light”, featuring Diamanda Galás, is the first taste of the follow-up, “Exaudire”, due on Metropolis Records on 22 January 2027.
items._cn_summary: Delerium即将发表新专辑《Exaudire》，延续了自1994年以来的合作模式：Bill Leeb与Rhys Fulber负责氛围化的电子制作骨架，再邀约不同客座歌手诠释慢速曲目。首支单曲《Into The Light》与美国前卫歌手Diamanda Galás合作，引用了她1986年专辑《The Divine Punishment》中《Deliver Me From Mine Enemies》的段落，将其嵌入Delerium自身的电子织体中。十二首曲目涵盖多位歌手客串，包括Mimi Page、Jaël、Inna Walters等。整体仍以暗潮、氛围电子为底色，融合了工业与前卫人声的边界探索。

items.body: An obsession, exaggeration Lust, desire and adoration Lose yourself in someone else Limerence closes every door Robots In Love have the sort of name that promises chrome-plated heartbreak, and their latest single Cease and Desist delivers an emotional sucker punch. The New Zealand dark electronic duo of vocalist-producer Elenor Rayner and drummer-producer Alex Burchell builds the song around obsession gone feral: attraction narrowing into fixation, fixation hardening into dependency, and reason getting shoved somewhere beneath the furniture. There is no polite exit once the appetite starts feeding on itself. The guitars come down hard, with hardcore licks driven right up against industrial metal without quite falling into Ministry cosplay. There is some of SINE’s bruising electronic pressure here, along with the blackened mechanical weight of latter-day Gary Numan, while the bigger synth architecture brushes against HEALTH, Nine Inch Nails, Sirus, and V.A.S.T. Burchell’s drumming has the clipped exactitude of somebody who has spent years learning how machines think, while Rayner sings from inside the mess those machines could never clean up. Desire behaves like bad wiring in the skull, making sleeplessness feel necessary and self-erasure almost reasonable. The chorus grows huge enough to suggest somebody shouting through concrete, yet the verses keep dragging the listener back toward the private humiliation of knowing exactly what is happening and remaining unable to stop it. “I recently discovered the word ‘limerence’ and started thinking about extreme obsession,” says Rayner. “Hence the line “limerence closes every door” where no amount of reasoning can get through. Musically, it’s got dark, heavy riffs, cinematic synths and an epic chorus.” The video, directed by Lichen Sorrel and Rayner, places the band inside a rain-soaked environment where reality keeps slipping sideways. Their movements feel slowed and strangely detached, as though the performers have wandered into somebody else’s private hallucination and decided to finish the set anyway. Watch the video for Cease and Desist below: Rayner has been working toward this collision for decades. She began playing Australian pubs on bass at fourteen before moving into electronic production on an Atari computer, “which opened up a universe of creating sounds and moulding them into rhythms and melodies until they evoke the exact feeling I need.” Her history runs through Soulscraper, Sobriquet, Snog, and The Crystalline Effect before Robots In Love took shape in New Zealand in 2017. Joined by Burchell in this current powerhouse incarnation, the project has developed a nasty elegance that can turn technical precision into emotional damage. With second album OVERRIDE ahead and guitarist Henry Flynn Wall joining the record, Cease and Desist makes obsession feel less romantic than chemical, compulsive, and absurd in the terrible way our worst impulses often are. Love may open doors, but limerence bolts them shut from the inside. Listen to Cease and Desist below and pre-order OVERRIDE here. items._cn_summary: 新西兰双人组合Robots In Love以单曲《Cease and Desist》呈现了一首关于执念失控的暗潮工业之作。歌曲以硬核吉他riff撞击工业金属边缘，配合沉重的电子压迫感，合成器架构向HEALTH与Nine Inch Nails靠拢。鼓机节奏精准如机械思维般锐利，人声却从情感的混乱内部倾泻而出。主歌与副歌形成张力对比，合唱庞大如穿透混凝土的呐喊，而主歌则将听者拉回清醒却无法自拔的羞耻感。MV以雨浸环境强化了现实的滑移与恍惚。乐队主唱Rayner从十四岁贝斯手到Atari电脑制作人，历经多个项目后形成当前形态。第二张专辑《OVERRIDE》即将发行，此曲预示了技术与情感破坏力的进一步碰撞。

items.body: I’ll see you in the vacant light Somewhere in-between In a room that my body makes For you and me Some songs announce themselves with a manifesto. Violet Silhouette’s This Is Something seems perfectly happy admitting that nobody involved has quite figured out what the hell is happening yet. A chant catches against a taut backbeat, bass and drums immediately putting bodies in motion while the synthesizers maintain a cooler distance. There is some early Human League in that contrast between machine discipline and romantic uncertainty, while the repetitive rhythmic pull recalls LCD Soundsystem at their most economical. Violet Silhouette leave plenty of room around the beat, allowing repetition to become its own persuasive force. Five minutes later you may still have questions, although sitting down probably will not be among them. This Is Something catches the instant before certainty settles in: two people meeting somewhere between confession and possibility, with a dance beat underneath them and enough unanswered questions to keep things interesting. The song began with rhythm. According to the band, the drums and beat drove its development while melodies were tested until the track revealed its peculiar identity. Compared with much of their forthcoming album, VIVID(IS)DECAY, This Is Something leans further into dance music, though its lyrics occupy considerably less certain territory. With Lily Vile joining on bass, Violet Silhouette now operates as a trio, and that expanded physical presence suits material built so firmly around movement. The group formed in West Palm Beach in late 2019 and has since become geographically divided between South Florida and Austin. Distance has become part of their method rather than an impediment, with Dan and Zaii exchanging early ideas for VIVID(IS)DECAY beginning in 2024. Night provides the setting, but clarity remains elusive. Someone is trying to make sense of where they have been while simultaneously wondering whether knowing would accomplish anything useful. Desire can be detected before it can be understood; feelings exist before language catches up with them. There is hesitation throughout the verses, coupled with a growing willingness to let another person see what has previously remained private. Then Violet Silhouette introduce one of the song’s strongest images: two people meeting somewhere between recognizable states, inside a private room formed by the body itself. Suddenly This Is Something feels less like an evasive title and more like an admission. Whatever this connection is, somebody has finally acknowledged its existence. The accompanying video carries the uncertainty somewhere considerably stranger. Violet Silhouette initially perform inside gorgeous neo-film-noir compositions, bodies moving with the backbeat before strobes, abstract tableaux, and blurred recollections begin interrupting any comfortable sense of reality. “Visually, we drew from David Lynch’s Lost Highway,” says the band. “Our friend Roberto Badillo took our vision and ran with it — the result is sleek and visceral, like a gloved hand dragging desire across the table.” That glove fits. Watch the video for This Is Something below: Produced, mixed, and mastered entirely by Violet Silhouette, VIVID(IS)DECAY explores what the band calls Neuromanticism, their pursuit of truth and love through unstable identities, secret languages, and emotional dissolution. Listen to This Is Something below and order the single here. items.body: Na skale Nad wodą Czaruje melodią For thousands of years, human beings have imagined voices calling to us from beyond the known world. The siren may be one of our oldest attempts to give desire a body. She waits at the boundary between land and sea, reason and longing, safety and surrender. Her song has power because the sailor brings something to it: loneliness, hope, curiosity, the wish to discover what lies beyond the horizon. Perhaps this is why the legend survives. The danger has never been merely the siren. It is our extraordinary capacity to hear, in the vast and indifferent world, precisely what we most wish were calling our name. Dawid Walkusz’s Syrena begins with the patience of something seen from a great distance: a bass line moving heavily beneath the surface, drums keeping a measured pace, and guitars and synths spreading a pale haze around Julia Frycz’s voice. The arrangement, channeling Current Joys, Cocteau Twins, Motorama, and Slowdive, belongs loosely to post-punk, coldwave, dreampop, and hypnagogic pop; though its strongest quality is less categorical than physical. The song seems to advance through water, every beat slightly burdened, every melodic phrase suspended between sleep and recognition. Frycz, a visual artist and vocalist with Emrere, gives Syrena its strange center of gravity. Her singing carries the calm authority of a figure who already knows how the story ends. Walkusz had written the instrumental and recorded early vocal parts before Frycz joined him, yet the collaboration feels unusually unified, as though both musicians had been picturing the same coastline without realizing it. Their subject is the siren, familiar from folklore as an emblem of beauty sharpened into danger, and the Polish lyrics render her with almost childlike clarity: she sits upon a rock above the water, her eyes glint, she appears angelic, and beneath the surface waits a tail. This simplicity gives the song room to become stranger. Sailors are drawn toward her by longing and tenderness, losing their way before affection itself becomes fatal. Walkusz and Frycz avoid turning the myth into theatrical gothic excess. The menace comes from softness, from the slow reassurance of the voice and the bass line’s stubborn tread. Desire becomes a navigational error. Love becomes a current capable of carrying someone farther than intended. The accompanying video extends this idea along the seaside, where cairns, stones, and open water create a setting suspended somewhere between Romantic poetry and Pre-Raphaelite painting. Frycz appears among the rocks as the siren, recalling the doomed women of Waterhouse and the river-bound Ophelia of Shakespeare, while Maciej Cimaszkiewicz’s cinematography favors natural forms over elaborate staging. Walkusz, who handled the editing and post-production, worked closely with Frycz to preserve the same visual language that had developed around the song. The shoreline becomes a psychological border, a place where the familiar world thins out and the sailor’s attraction begins to resemble surrender. Watch Syrena below: Syrena is the first glimpse of Walkusz’s second solo album, Fantometyka, due in spring 2027, and it suggests a broader, more confident development from his debut, Monochrom. The earlier record established his attraction to austere rhythms and blurred textures; here, those elements have acquired a more sensual sense of space. The song moves slowly, almost ceremonially, and its danger lies in how comfortable that pace becomes. By the time the siren has finished singing, the sailor’s fate feels less like catastrophe than consent. Listen to Syrena below, and order the single here. items._cn_summary: 波兰音乐人Dawid Walkusz与视觉艺术家兼歌手Julia Frycz合作的单曲《Syrena》，以希腊神话中的海妖为意象核心。Frycz的声音冷静而具有预知性，与厚重的贝斯线、缓慢推进的鼓点和弥漫的吉他与合成器雾气形成呼应，音乐在水下般的质地中展开，融合了冷波、梦幻流行与半梦半醒流行的质感。波兰语歌词以近乎孩童般的清澈笔触描绘海妖的诱惑与危险——她坐于岩石之上，眼睛闪光，尾鳍潜伏于水下。歌曲拒绝戏剧化的哥特式夸张，其威胁感来自柔软、来自声音与贝斯的缓慢保证。MV由Maciej Cimaszkiewicz掌镜，呈现海岸边石堆与开阔水面构成的场景，Frycz作为海妖出现，影像语言接近拉斐尔前派与浪漫主义诗歌之间的过渡地带。整体呈现出梦境与神话交汇的听觉与视觉诗学。

items.body: Ten years is a long time to leave a monster in the basement, especially when you know it has been down there learning new tricks. Ghosts In The Graveyard return to their 2016 debut, Monsters For The Masses, with the zeal of directors who finally found the budget they wanted the first time around. Monsters For The Masses: Resurrected tears into the old recordings with fresh programming, heavier production, electronic detail, and the accumulated bad habits of a band that has spent a decade getting better at making darkness dance. The real kick comes from hearing Byron C. Miller’s younger self dragged into the present without sanding away the cheap-horror charm. Miller had just come out of eight years with God Module when the original record took shape, and you can still feel a frontman figuring out how much theater, electronics, guitar damage, and personal debris he could cram into his own clubhouse. “This album means the world to me,” gushes Miller. “After 8 years in God Module, this was the first music project I put together, the first time I was writing most of the lyrics, defining the aesthetic. The interludes on this album are made from cassette recordings I did when I was a little kid trying to be scary. In many ways these songs are the first half of my life as song. I’m so glad that my bandmate, music creator, Paul Morgan, was able to take everything he’s learned and go in and rebuild these tracks from the original recordings. I love how these new mixes were mastered by our pal, Chris Longo. This is how the album was always meant to sound!” Directed by Byron C. Miller and shot by cinematographer Paul Morgan, the Monster Mask video follows an eerie little vignette in which a woman’s peace is abruptly disturbed. We’ll leave the rest of the plot buried where it belongs, since spoiling horror is the cultural equivalent of telling somebody what is inside the coffin before they pry it open. One practical warning, however: the video contains extensive flashing lights, so viewers with photosensitivity should approach accordingly. Watch the video for Monster Mask: Resurrected below: Ghosts In The Graveyard know horror works best when somebody is having too much fun with it. “Better In Black: Resurrected Version” comes back with its teeth filed to fresh points, Paul Morgan rebuilding the track from the original masters while preserving the sleazy romantic pull that made it central to the band’s identity. Monster Mask: Resurrected Version sinks lower and stranger, bringing dark trip-hop tension into the graveyard. Then there is Debonair, the sole new recording, a cover of The Afghan Whigs that gives the project its best excuse for existing beyond anniversary bookkeeping. It has the heat of a band testing an old skeleton under stage lights, turning the album into a current document with ten years of dirt under its fingernails. Ghosts In The Graveyard still love blood, monsters, desire, death, and all the lurid furniture, yet the stronger point is how seriously they take the pleasure of performance. Resurrection becomes vandalism with better equipment, a chance to exhume their younger selves, hand them louder machinery, and see what starts moving. Listen to Monster Mask: Resurrected below and purchase the single here. Miller此前在God Module待了八年，这张专辑对他而言意味着独立创作生涯的开端，专辑间隙段插入了儿时用磁带录制的音效素材。重制版保留了原作的廉价恐怖片魅力，同时让旧作听感更现代。另外收录了一首The Afghan Whigs的翻唱《Debonair》，是新作中唯一的全新录音，为这张周年纪念专辑注入了当下的活力。整体定位是恐怖美学加电子节拍的暗潮工业融合，对暗潮和工业音乐爱好者具有一定吸引力。

items.body: Curses Perfect High Altered Circuits Luca Venezia is a tastemaker DJ and producer in the classic mold; via his remixes, curation as the selector behind the superlative Next Wave Acid Punx compilations, and his releases CURSES, the Berlin based artist has been forging a varied, but consistent blend of darkwave, disco, EBM that keeps an eye to the dancefloor but doesn’t skimp on the atmosphere. On Perfect High Venezia digs deep into the new beat and NRG sounds that have informed his work, leaning heavily on funky rhythm programming for grooves. The title track doesn’t waste much time, establishing a big shuffling rhythm accented by orch hits, buzzy synth bass and stabs of sampled guitar to carry the track, its melody limited a simple repeating synth 3 note synth figure and repeated vocals. “Killer Instinct” strips everything down drums and e-bass, much of its texture found in the delay and reverb trails that follow its metallic perc hits and vocal samples. The new beat influence really comes to a head on “Dare 2 Dream”, where a brassy lead flies above pitched and chopped samples and a simple but effect kick-snare pattern, rolling hard at a dancefloor friendly mid-tempo rhythm. CURSES rarely misses, and given how in his wheelhouse Perfect High is, he wasn’t about to start here. Curses – Perfect High EP by Curses Transmigration Living Information self-released London act Transmigration has an immediate rush of nostalgic appeal on recent EP Living Information. Anyone cursorily familiar with electro-industrial will feel immediately at ease with the mix of echoing programming, samples, and vocals which reverberate through the title track or closer “Convergence” – a healthy balance of composition and production ensures that the acid panache of those tracks never oversteps the solid grooves at their base. But spend a bit more time with the EP and you’ll be impressed by how Transmigration’s able to call back to the antecedents of that style as well as bring it into the present without losing their own personality. “Ceaseless” carries a familiarly furtive 242 style forward via the like of Visitor and other modern lo-fi stylists, while the stuttering electro kicks of “Understanding” suggest either Kontravoid or (real heads remember) By Any Means Necessary. That’s a pretty wide historical spread, but Transmigration’s vocal personality as well as their yen for wet, dark electro reverb links those respective points along a thirty-plus year history quite handily. Fun, chewy, and satisfying listening for those who know their history. Living Information by Transmigration The post Observer: Curses & Transmigration appeared first on I Die: You Die.
items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评以观察栏目的形式介绍了两位电子音乐人的新作。Curses 的《Perfect High》EP 深植于新派节拍与NRG传统，以funky节奏编程为核心，合成器贝斯与采样吉他层层堆叠，整体偏向舞池取向又不失氛围营造；其中《Dare 2 Dream》以铜管质感的领奏声部凸显新派节拍影响。Transmigration 的《Living Information》则更具回溯色彩，标题曲与《Convergence》在回响编程与人声采样间取得平衡，酸性音色不失扎实底鼓；《Ceaseless》呈现类似Front 242的潜行气质，《Understanding》的顿挫电鼓节拍则让人联想到Kontravoid或早期工业经典。两组作品均显示出在三十余年历史脉络中整合前辈影响并保持个人辨识度的能力，定位明确，制作扎实。

items.body: Music For Drifting is the debut LP from Aase Frejadóttir. Releasing on Editions Verde, and using synthesizers, field recordings, strings, and voice, Frejadóttir’s music isn’t afraid to switch things up. Straight off the bat, her music feels incredibly expansive while also remaining intimate and warm. There’s no doubt that the warmth is due to the synth, and it radiates from it, but its soft swells and the emergence of a new melody also helps to provide a benevolent atmosphere of awe and wonder that fits in with the warmer sound. Whether walking her dog, Pulsar, or drifting through the forests on the outskirts of Stockholm, Aase’s music appears to be a free spirit, in search of something more: extracting deeper meanings from the music, which is a glowing stream of distant light. A lover of Astronomy from an early age, Aase’s music is interwoven with the black fabric of space, containing material from an infinite beyond, and she builds her spacious music upon its bedrock – the glowing light of dead stars and something of the cosmic is audible in her music. Strings burst forth and a radiant harmony bursts onto the scene with the royal elegance, grace, and supreme force of a bejewelled supernova. Her music is constantly shifting, turning, its refractions and reflections rebounding and moving from note-to-note. Everything is tied to the Universe and the greater unknown, but although wide open arms and spatial possibilities are present on Music For Drifting, Aase never loses touch with what she and seven billion others call home, as heard in the more familiar, meteorological music of rain. That deluge of rain opens up ‘Dimma Promenad’, bringing us back to the soil and the earth, before transitioning into standout piece ‘Solemn Oath’ – twenty minutes of sweeping, orchestrated movements and patient drones. Cascading melodies glint and gently oscillate, and although the piece centres on a cluster of notes, it manages to evoke a ton of space and a reverential air fitting for a sacred oath. The notes are as pure and blessed as Holy Water. Following on is ‘Aerial’, which, with its additional layering, immediately counter-balances the previous piece. It favours depth over a skeletal fragility, and plump notes over a slimmer variant. Companionship and friendship over a solitary, long-forgotten corner of space, like the Earth’s positioning in the Milky Way. The mood is one of reflection and contemplation, not looking to figure things out with scientific equations or facts about the Universe, but rather revelling in its being. One can believe in the theory of an animated Universe when listening to her music. It’s enjoying existence for what it is: glorious, painful, tragic, thrilling. EV008: Music for Drifting by Aase Frejadóttir www.editionsverde.bandcamp.com

items._cn_summary: 这张首张专辑以合成器、田野录音、弦乐与人声为素材，构建出广阔而温暖的声音空间。创作深受天文学与北欧自然环境影响，森林漫步、雨水声效、犬只陪伴等日常意象被编织进宇宙尺度的沉思中。专辑在轨道编排上呈现明显的张力对比：二十多分钟的《Solemn Oath》以管弦乐式涌动与耐心持续音为主轴，音符纯净庄严；紧随其后的《Aerial》则转向层次纵深与丰盈质感，暗示陪伴与友谊的主题。整体声响在不同曲段间不断折射、转折，既拥抱未知又扎根于大地，将天文学的敬畏感转化为可聆听的声音流。

items.body:
After the OĽUN album I reviewed enthusiastically a while back, here’s the next project, again motivated and led by violinist/fiddler/composer Ján Kružliak Jr., continuing the rapprochement, indeed embrace, between Slovakia’s traditional music and its classical music. This time it reconnects the works of classical composers who were inspired by and drew on village musics with those traditional sources and styles.
Three ensembles are involved: the Spectrum Quartett led by Kru�liak with two violins, viola and cello; Nogaband, the traditional-style quartet of fiddles, contra (chording viola) and bass that’s led by fiddler and singer Michal Noga; and the female vocal group Ulijanky, plus guest singer Simona Hulejov�.
The majority of the tracks are interpretations of works by Slovak composer Eugen Suchon (1908-1993), with others from fellow-Slovaks Ilja Zeljenka (1932-2007) and Alexander Moyzes (1906-1984), and Hungarian B�la Bart�k (1881-1945) who did a lot of his very detailed collecting of folk music in Slovakia.
In each case the sources - musicians and locations in villages across Slovakia - are credited in the notes, and these arrangements and performances reconnect with the energy and traditional vocal sound of those sources.
In no way is this an orchestra-smoothed thing; this is gutsy, brilliantly played and sung music with all the spirit, skill and technique of traditional music, from players and singers who deeply understand and inhabit it. It’s a glorious piece of work, music to luxuriate in. There’s too much richness to begin to detail, but here’s a dip into a few moments to give the flavor. The tracks all have very long titles detailing their sources, so for brevity’s sake I’ll just give track numbers.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由小提琴家Ján Kružliak Jr.主导，旨在重新连接斯洛伐克传统民间音乐与古典音乐传统。参与演奏的三个团体各具特色：Spectrum Quartett提供弦乐四重奏的古典基底，Nogaband以小提琴、对位中音提琴与贝斯呈现民间合奏形态，Ulijanky女声合唱团则承载传统声乐素材。曲目主要改编自斯洛伐克作曲家Eugen Suchoň、Ilja Zeljenka、Alexander Moyzes以及曾在斯洛伐克大量采集民谣的匈牙利作曲家Béla Bartók的作品，每首曲目都标注了具体的村落音乐来源。编曲与演奏保留了传统音乐的粗粝感与能量，并非经过管弦乐打磨的平滑处理。专辑展现了古典作曲家从民间汲取灵感后，作品如何重新与原始素材和风格产生对话的过程。

items.body:
Though this recording documents the work of thirteen of Belgium's most innovative ensembles, the real star is the Park Abbey located just outside Leuven and founded in 1129. Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhythms, and accordion-based
bal-musette
flavors.
For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.
Find out more about Merodefestival.
Further reading and listening
Piet Maris and Sarah Baur talk about the artist collective Choux de Bruxelles
(Interview)

Songbooks Live
(Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑收录了十三支比利时创新乐团的作品，录制于1129年建立的帕克修道院中，演奏家们在古老的石质建筑内利用天然混响完成录音。专辑以器乐为主，融合比利时民间音乐与世界音乐传统，涵盖罗姆人音阶、bal-musette手风琴风格、地中海与阿拉伯元素。Rénélus Bikar以小提琴开场，追溯泛欧罗姆人历史；Charlotte Pelgen以班卓琴般的尤克里里演绎Django Reinhardt式的摇摆乐；黎巴嫩裔歌手Amber Haddad与乌德琴手合作，展现东方色彩。Andries Boone的曼陀林与羽管键琴组合带来近似巴洛克的声音质感。整张专辑风格跨度宽广却保持内在统一，修道院的冥想氛围贯穿始终，录音历时三年，制作精良。

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑聚焦于俄乌冲突中被绑架的约两万乌克兰儿童这一沉重主题，由乌克兰裔加拿大歌手Marichka与加拿大全女子团体Daughters of Donbas共同演绎。音乐以传统弓弦乐器、班杜拉琴和钢琴为核心，融合传统民歌与原创作品，在加拿大和乌克兰两地录制完成。专辑中包含一位曾被绑架后成功归来的16岁Mariupol少女演奏双陶笛的段落。第一轨《Foreign Land》以温和的声线翻唱一首关于被送往异乡做工的少女的传统歌谣，而第二轨《Rusalka》则转向激烈强悍的唱腔，取材于斯拉夫民间传说中的自然精灵。评论者强调专辑在音乐与人声层面均具有扎实水准，无需同情预设也能作为纯粹音乐来感受，而阅读歌词后更深受触动。

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Various Artists - L�ve L�ve (Volume1) (Review) Pedro Lima - Maguidala (Review) Ann O'aro - Bleu (Review)
items.label: Bongo Joe
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑聚焦圣多美和普林西比七十至八十年代的Puxa舞曲，这一音乐流派融合了来自其他非洲葡语国家的节奏元素，混合merengue、Kompas、Soukouss、Benga等多种风格。乐评指出该岛国虽小，但其音乐展现出强烈的舞蹈驱动力与即兴延展能力，吉他与鼓组的交织构成核心肌理，多把吉他相互缠绕，主唱与和声在旋律框架内持续对话，乐段常常在现场的演绎中无限延伸。评论特别提到Pedro Lima领衔的乐队以闷音吉他的切分riff与鼓手对位，Sangazuza则展示了贝斯与键盘退出后鼓与吉他主导的迷幻律动。整体属于独立小厂牌Bongo Joe的非洲音乐再发掘项目，从文化研究角度具有独特视角。

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. More to hear: United States of Alchemy - Songs of Compassion (Review) Dani Jan� - Vida (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以中提琴、簧风琴、击弦古钢琴和钢琴为核心乐器，加入鼓、贝斯和合成器层，音乐多为一次即兴录制完成。作品融合民谣、前卫音乐与宗教氛围，在持续嗡鸣的底色上搭建旋律线，部分曲目取材于古老民歌或中世纪圣咏的质感。作为对已故父亲的纪念专辑，弥漫着深沉而克制的哀思，结尾关于父亲最后一次前往他钟爱的小块菜地的曲目尤为动人。光与暗在不同曲目间交替渗透，情绪流动自然。整体风格游离于既有分类之外，既具备前卫视角又保留了旋律可听性，对寻求跨界融合的听众而言是一次兼具挑战性与满足感的聆听体验。

items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张合辑聚焦贝宁歌手兼巫毒实践者Antoine Dougbé与Orchestre Poly-Rythmo在1977至1982年间的合作录音。Dougbé以拍手演绎Cavacha节奏著称，这种由鼓手Belobi Meridjo从火车节奏演变而来的律动后广泛传入中部非洲流行乐。乐评详细介绍了Analog Africa厂牌多年来对Poly-Rythmo资料的整理脉络，并指出本辑与其他Poly-Rythmo合辑的区别在于受古巴son影响的痕迹更明显，尤其在开篇几首中体现。曲目《Ma Won Min Towe Leo》以合成器铺底，吉他音色带有塑料光泽的八十年代质感，高帽主导的律动贯穿始终。文中还提到刚果伦巴对撒哈拉以南非洲的冲击，Dougbé虽录音生涯短暂，三张专辑和几首单曲却展现了鲜明的个性。整体属于世界音乐范畴中带有部落信仰与跨大西洋律动对话的跨界作品。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items._cn_summary: 这是挪威Camilla Hole Trio在先前专辑将科幻合成器与传统民乐嫁接之后推出的新作，整体回归更为踏实的地面感，但依然延续了超越本土民乐语汇的探索。主创乐器为高音萨克斯，爵士影响明显，首曲即以挪威西部的春之舞曲旋律展开。乐队三人角色界限模糊，Kalman的低音提琴既提供节奏支撑也加入模块合成器音色，Nesheim的鼓与颤音琴交替推进，三人不断交换主旋律与即兴位置，使作品呈现出开放式的流动结构。专辑将挪威传统民谣素材与爵士即兴手法融合，并辅以电子音色拓展声场，介于学院爵士与世界音乐跨界之间，适合对北欧实验爵士与民谣融合感兴趣的听众。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由一位瑞典小提琴家和两位挪威演奏家组成的三重奏，对斯堪的纳维亚传统舞曲进行了非常规的重新诠释。乐评将其比作室内乐——三位演奏者沉浸在亲密的音乐对话中，揭示舞曲表面欢快之下的不安暗流。专辑以挪威塞特斯达尔山谷的传说小提琴曲"Fossgrimen"开篇，呼应民间传说中的水妖与魔鬼乐器意象。Tellef Kvifte 主要用竖笛和萨克斯引领旋律，其子 Knut 担任鼓手与作曲，三人模糊了民间音乐与其他流派之间的界限。编曲突破舞蹈伴奏功能，转向探索音乐深层意味，短曲"Per Myhr 的波兰舞曲"展示了旋律从齐奏到分崩离析的转变。Taragot 厂牌的小众独立发行契合实验性世界音乐定位。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A reunion, of sorts, in effect as all participants in this studio product had played with Jack in former bands; The Graham Bond Quartet (Bruce & McLaughlin), The Graham Bond Organization (Bruce & Heckstall-Smith), and Jack's previous album, Songs for a Tailor (with Hiseman). (Hiseman and Heckstall-Smith had, of course, been playing for a couple years together in David Greenslade's Colosseum--three albums worth.)1. "Over The Cliff" (2:56) a quick riff from Dick Heckstall-Smith's tenor sax launches bassist Jack Bruce and drummer Jon Hiseman into a rapid-paced expression of fairly straightforward Hard Bop Jazz. There is little to no input from John McLaughlin's guitar but Dick, Jack, and Jon are more than up for the trio presentation. Interesting and respected but this is not really my preferred type of music. (8.875/10)2. "Statues" (7:35) more blues-based Hard Bop Jazz from Dick, Jack, and Jon in which the trio dance around one another in tight and attentive circles, each playing their own consistent melody lines--Dick even going for the two-saxes in the mouth at the same time trick a couple times. In the fifth minute there is a cease and desist order so that Jack can bow his bass a bit, but then Jon rejoins with meagre little input from Dick (and, interestingly, none from John McLaughlin) before Jack steps back to let Jon have the spotlight a couple of times before the recapitulation of the opening themes over the final 35 seconds. Fine musicianship. (13.5/15)3. "Sam Enchanted Dick" - medley (7:28) bass and electric guitar recite the song's main melodies over Jon's drums for the first 30+ seconds before John is loosed with his distorted tone to solo for about a minute. Then it's Jack's turn in the third minute. John's chord accents are all I can pay attention to (for I am a HUGE fan of John's fascinating "rhythm guitar" choices). At 3:37 we hear the first squirts of Dick's, tenor sax--which leads, of course, to an extended solo for him (and yet my ears still find themselves paying attention to John's caustic chord interjections). Double saxes for a bit in the seventh minute before Dick's play on "Sweet Georgia Brown" lead to the song's finish. (13.5/15) a. "Sam Sack" b. "Rill's Thrills"4. "Born To Be Blue" (4:26) a gorgeous ballad with very sensitive performances from all four players. There is enough space in the soundscape of this song that I can very much appreciate the skills and creativity of each individual musician--which I need from time to time in order to better understand and value the musics I'm being exposed to. (9/10)5. "HCKHH Blues" (8:59) there is an auspicious threat of power and havoc in this song's music from its very opening. Despite Jack and John's pulling tendency to want to drift over into the Louisiana Bayous, Dick and Jon do a great job in keeping the spirit firmly anchored in less Southern traditions, more in the urban forms of expression. Finally pusuaded, John and Jack swing over to join Dick and John in their Coltrane-like explorations. (18.125/20)6. "Ballad For Arthur" (7:42) pensive bass notes are embellished by delicate cymbal and snare play while Dick explores his own melody ideas. There is enough focus in Dick's playing that Jack and Jon both feel empowered to let their own playing go a bit into the realms of improvisational freedom--until, that is, John feels inspired to join in (around 1:50). Thereafter John's "commanding presence" effects a stoppage from Jon (no drums or cymbal sound for over a minute!) while Dick tries to figure out how to play background accompanist role to John's spacial musings. With Jon's boisterous Jack DeJohnette-like return in the fifth minute, we find the other three suddenly inspired to become quite a bit more dynamic: each flying off in their own directions while somehow it all still manages to make sense from a collective view. With a minute left to go there is a sudden buildup and burst into controlled chaos before everybody backs out, spent. While I still don't "like" this kind of music, I understand anad appreciate the discipline and skill required to make it happen--to make it work. (13.5/15)7. "Things We Like" (3:38) another this time more targeted and speedy foray into the reactive/responsive side of Jazz' free jazz movement. There is a playfulness to this one that makes it a bit more amusing and, thus, enjoyable. (8.875/10)Total Time 48:04Despite the presence (and influence) of metamorphosizing guitarist John McLaughlin on four of the album's seven songs, the rest of the band on this album (Bruce, Hiseman, and Heckstall-Smith) are all playing Jazz, standard, blues-based Jazz albeit at times what we've come to call their own versions of "free jazz." John is the only one pushing boundaries, injecting non-standard sounds, riffs, and epithets. One might also argue that Dick Heckstall-Smith is pushing for more free jazz representation. Were I more of fan of straight Jazz (I'm trying, folks!) I might like this album more. As it stands, I feel hard-pressed to even consider this "Jazz-Rock Fusion" much less call it such.B+/4.5 stars; while Jazz afficionadoes might consider this a minor masterpiece of Jazz (or even Jazz-Rock Fusion), would call this a near-masterpiece and not a true representative of Jazz-Rock Fusion; to my mind Things We Like has got far more of the fire and focus of pure Jazz than it does of Fusion or progressive rock.
items._cn_summary: 这张1970年的专辑汇集了Jack Bruce、John McLaughlin、Dick Heckstall-Smith和Jon Hiseman四位英国爵士/摇滚乐手，是Graham Bond乐队时期合作的延伸。整体以硬波普爵士为基础，融合蓝调、放克与早期爵士摇滚元素，编曲注重即兴对话与乐器间的互动。低音声部由Jack Bruce的贝斯主导，无论是拨弦还是拉弓都展现细腻技巧；McLaughlin的吉他以节奏切音和偶尔的失真独奏点缀；Heckstall-Smith的次中音萨克斯承担主旋律线条，常运用双萨克斯同时吹奏技巧。专辑在硬波普框架内加入自由段落和成员间的轮换独奏，既保留传统爵士语汇，也透露出向爵士摇滚过渡的实验倾向，适合爵士乐迷和关注英国爵士摇滚起源的听众。
