items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — At the time, I thought Strange Little Girls was the last album where Tori Amos pursued a specific stylistic direction; just as she had previously dedicated albums to the sound of the acoustic piano or the clavichord, here she focused on the Wurlitzer (alongside her classic B�sendorfer piano), which gave the record a very special atmosphere. Yet that wasn't the only thing distinguishing the �lbum, which was dedicated to covering songs originally performed by men and giving them a feminine twist. However, rather than focusing on the personas she created for each track, I want to concentrate on the music itself; each version is distinct and received such a unique treatment, akin to applying makeup, that the song was transformed until it became unrecognizable, turning into something entirely new. This reveals the true meaning of reimagining a song."New Age", originally by The Velvet Underground, is transported to another dimension: a cold, futuristic realm, ripped without anesthesia from its quasi-hippie, Buffalo Springfield-esque setting. Tori sings with restraint at first before letting go; her voice sounds perfect alongside the album's other star, guitarist Adrian Belew. While the original held the light of morning, she imbued this version with the shadow of dusk, its diametric opposite.Belew helps make the album more challenging and progressive; his riffs complement the spirit of Tori, which was already unconventional for the time. Then there is "'97 Bonnie & Clyde", originally by rapper Eminem, though it goes without saying that the song is unrecognizable here. It is subtle and modern, yet simultaneously evokes the 1920s, featuring a drum machine that contrasts with the sound of violins and her whispered vocals.The case of "Strange Little Girls" is intriguing; for its creators, The Stranglers, it represented a move toward modernity, embracing new wave after their punk past, while Amos takes it a step further by making it postmodern. The Wurlitzer lends a futuristic air, and her committed, uninhibited vocal performance, bolstered by backing vocals, truly makes the song her own. Matt Chamberlain provides the final touch that perfects the power of this rendition.Depeche Mode's "Enjoy the Silence" is so powerful that one need not dig deep to unlock its full potential. Stripped of all its trappings, just the song itself, a piano, and a few strings, it shone like a mineral catching a ray of sunlight, glowing even from afar.She took 10cc's 1975 track "I'm Not In Love", originally warm and even contradictorily (or paradoxically) romantic, and made it icy, almost Krautrock-esque and mechanical; it features a long introduction where the beautiful original melody is recognizable only in her vocals, yet here it feels more like a threat, even though the original lyrics seemed like a confession born of denial."Rattlesnakes", a song by Lloyd Cole and the Commotions, also retains its original melody, though the tempo has been slowed down; the country, road-trip vibe remains, driven by the sound of the Rhodes piano. However, while the original's string arrangements gave it a friendly, Waterboys-esque feel, this version seems more rooted in the rural landscape of Wim Wenders' "Paris, Texas", which, at the very least, imbues it with genuine emotion."Time", by my dear Tom Waits and taken from the album Rain Dogs, remains completely unchanged; no alteration was needed, as the only shift here lay (significantly) in the vocals. Tom's voice carries powerful tones and deep emotion, tinged with melancholy in this instance, while Tori's version holds its own distinct nuances, rooted in a similarly somber quality but stemming from different sources.Neil Young and his album Harvest need no introduction; they make even those of us who aren't huge fans of country music love it!, And Tori interpreted it as if she were Garbage, with a Portishead-style trip-hop vibe, distorting, transforming, and rocking it out, much like Neil Young had transformed Bob Dylan's "All Along the Watchtower." A double tribute."I Don't Like Mondays", the iconic ballad by The Boomtown Rats (Bob Geldof's band), was a chamber-pop track featuring distinctly New Wave strings, a rich, elaborate sound, and prominent piano work. Tori captured the song's essence while performing solo on the Rhodes; she made it more direct and sincere, less explosive, and instead, something akin to an implosion."Happiness Is A Warm Gun" (originally by The Beatles, of course) features a prominent contribution from Belew, recalling his years alongside Robert Fripp, and evokes the atmosphere of his solo album Exposure, in which the guitar intermingles with audio snippets of George W. Bush; much like Fripp's record, which also incorporated overlaid audio, this concept album cemented modernity as the norm. There is plenty of room for improvisation here, and the creative flight turns progressive once again, with a psychedelic, spacey and cosmic feel.Slayer's "Raining Blood" made people headbang and stomp along to the beat... Tori's version seems to have descended into a netherworld where neither time nor physical matter exists; consequently, it feels and is perceived differently. Her piano is deep and low, it inflicts pain (were we capable of feeling it), and her voice possesses a density equal to that of the guitars in the original. If Slayer's intention was to evoke fear, this version inspires terror.We come to the final track, one by another pianist I greatly admire, Joe Jackson: "Real Men," a classic from his album Night & Day that he always performed live. The original 1982 version already featured a drum machine, keyboards, and an uptempo beat, yet it was imbued with deep emotion through Joe's performance. Consequently, Tori didn't need to alter the song's spirit; aside from performing it as a solo piano piece, an approach she took throughout the album, modifying arrangements only when necessary, she made choices that I feel were spot-on. Just as Joe is a brilliant pianist, so is she; she infused the song with her own piano sensibility, incorporating a few additional classical-style notes. And so, in a manner that feels almost sarcastic given the final track's title and the album's overarching theme, yet while remaining deeply faithful to the defiant spirit of many of the original songs, these twelve covers found a new home.
items._genre: art pop / progressive pop / experimental covers / avant-folk
items._cn_summary: 这是Tori Amos 2001年发行的翻唱专辑，以女性视角重新诠释十首原由男性演绎的歌曲。她以Wurlitzer电钢琴搭配Bösendorfer三角琴，营造出冷峻而独特的氛围。每首翻唱都进行了深度的解构与重塑：The Velvet Underground的New Age被推向冰冷未来主义领域，Eminem的'97 Bonnie & Clyde以1920年代风格与电子鼓机并置，The Stranglers的同名曲走向后现代，10cc的I'm Not In Love被处理成机械冷感的近似Krautrock质感，Deche Mode的Enjoy the Silence则被极致精简至钢琴与弦乐。吉他手Adrian Belew的加入为整体增添了前卫色彩与挑战性。整张专辑的核心在于完全消解原作面貌，使听者无法辨认原始版本，重新定义翻唱行为的意义。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The trio format suits the Canterbury scene perfectly. Soft Machine immediately comes to mind, yet a jazz sensibility permeates the French group's sound, whether through the piano or the Hammond organ. As with Soft Machine, vocals are not their strong suit; during the instrumental sections of "Voici la nuit tomb�e," they also lean into a Doors-esque psychedelia.While the classic distorted keyboard sound sets the mood, Yves Hasselmann's vocals occasionally flirt with a classical style reminiscent of Supersister, until the jazz trio element takes over. Atonal passages build great suspense and a French film noir atmosphere, fittingly enough, eventually giving way to further psychedelic sections.However, in other passages, the composition is less daring, settling into a more conventional jazz style akin to that of the previous decade. "Flamenco" follows jazz-style counterpoint, adding Canterbury-esque humor in the vein of Supersister and pushing the sonic boundaries of the trio, with outstanding work from bassist Jacques-Edmond Gour�."Passo" reminded me of Friedrich Gulda's preludes, before shifting into an improvisation more in the style of Keith Jarrett. "Soleil" bears a strong resemblance to Dave Brubeck and "Blue Rondo � la Turk"; the format of short, consecutive tracks suits the trio well following the eighteen-minute suite, as immediacy and speed were Paramount, the idea being that he who strikes first strikes twice, even if they couldn't quite sustain the dramatic tension achieved by their counterparts in Moving Gelatine Plates. The surrealist element was tempered by a classic jazz sensibility that took a bit of the intensity out of the Project, though certainly not its value or quality.
items._genre: Canterbury scene / jazz rock / psychedelic / experimental
items._cn_summary: 这是法国乐队 TRAVELLING 于1973年发行的专辑，以钢琴、哈蒙德风琴与贝斯的三重奏形式展开，融合坎特伯雷场景的爵士摇滚特质与法国新浪潮式的黑色电影氛围。十八分钟的同名长曲中，无调性段落构建悬疑张力，失真键盘音色带出门户乐队式的迷幻色彩，随后转入相对传统的爵士段落。贝斯手 Gouré 的反行爵士对位在 Flamenco 一曲中尤为突出。Passo 让人联想到 Friedrich Gulda 的前奏曲与 Keith Jarrett 的即兴，Soleil 则呼应 Dave Brubeck 的经典曲目。多首短曲的结构切换带来即时性，但整体超现实色彩被传统爵士感性所冲淡，削弱了强度。评论将其定位为 Soft Machine 与 Supersister 的法国同侪，风格独特但稍欠锐利。

items.body: “The devil is busy” is what churchgoers say when trouble arrives, and Seun Kuti & Egypt 80 take the phrase, as “Devil Just Busy”, and point it at the darkness closing over contemporary society. Seun turns the preachers’ own words back on them: on the title track and first single of his upcoming album Na Dem, he already listed reverends, bishops, pastors and imams among the “winch men” he wants saving from, and his father Fela Kuti went after the same pulpits on “Shuffering and Shmiling” in 1978. “DJB” gives the phrase seven minutes of dark, mid-tempo afrobeat, laid down by two drummers, Mario Orsinet and Femi Koleoso, and two bassists, Kunle Justice and Gbeke Ojutiku. Seun sings and plays saxophone on top, with two trumpets and four more saxophones building the horn arrangements around him. Koleoso, who leads Ezra Collective, also produced the track, as he did the whole of Na Dem. Na Dem arrives on 6 November via Django Music, eight days before Fela becomes the first African solo artist inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Seun, who inherited Egypt 80 at 14 when his father died in 1997, will be in Los Angeles to represent him at the ceremony, five weeks after the band play the city’s Regent Theater on 9 October. That date sits in a US run that also takes in Belly Up Tavern in Solana Beach on 7 October, FORM Arcosanti in Arizona and Webster Hall in New York on 14 October. items.body: Soft Riot has finished a video for “Ghostwriter,” the closing track on the 2026 album “Crux.” It is the project’s second official video from the record, following “Moving Out Of The Black,” which premiered at the end of April 2026 ahead of the album’s release on 15 May. A premiere date for “Ghostwriter” itself is still being finalised; the video is not yet public. Crux by Soft Riot Jack Duckworth, who records as Soft Riot and is also known as JJD, built the video’s visuals as a graphic, surrealist collage rather than a straight performance piece, with puppet-like character animation reflecting the song’s theme: the sense of ideas for “Crux” materialising, as though something unseen were “ghostwriting” the record. All of the animation was made by hand from physically printed graphics and re-filmed projected textures, a deliberate move away from computer-based tools that Duckworth has linked to feeling increasingly isolated within the digital side of underground music. Duckworth handled all graphics and editing as JJD, with assistance from Leyre Mann Vadillo. “Ghostwriter” closes a nine-track album written and recorded across several sessions between June 2024 and January 2026 at Studio Carillon in Glasgow, with vinyl mixing by Owen Pratt at Flesh And Bone Studios in Tarn, France, and mastering by Josh Stevenson at Otic Mastering. “Crux” is available on streaming platforms, as a download through Bandcamp and Subvert via Possession Records, and on vinyl and digipak CD, including a limited clear vinyl LP on Minimal Kombinat that sold out within a week of pre-orders. A follow-up EP, “Alter,” released in June 2026, carries exclusive, alternate and extended versions of “Crux” material. About Soft Riot Soft Riot is the synth project of Jack Duckworth, a British-Canadian musician based in Glasgow who has released music under the name for around fifteen years, drawing on synth post-punk, darkwave, new wave, Italo and EBM. Duckworth’s roots go back to the mid-1990s art-punk and hardcore scene on the North American west coast, where he played in the first-wave post-punk revival band Radio Berlin (1998-2005) and the industrial synth-punk group A Luna Red (Gold Standard Labs, 1999-2003). As Soft Riot, he has toured Europe repeatedly, sharing stages with acts including Front 242, Absolute Body Control, Parade Ground, She Past Away, Test Department, Selofan, Drab Majesty and Lebanon Hanover, and has played festivals including Ombra Festival in Spain, BIM Fest and Waveteef in Belgium, Kalabalik På Tyrolen in Sweden and Weird Science in Germany. Side-Line has previously covered the Soft Riot albums “You Never Know What Might Come Next” (2016), “The Outsider In The Mirrors” (2018) and “When Push Comes To Shove” (2019), followed by “No.” (2023) and, in 2026, “Crux” and its “Alter” companion EP.

items.body: When Side-Line spoke with Rina Pavar in 2023, live performance was still something she approached from outside: the studio was familiar territory, while putting herself physically at the centre of the music remained a challenge. Three years later, watching her open Saturday at Nocturnal Culture Night on the Parkbühne, in daylight and before the festival had fully gathered momentum, the change was striking. The restraint was still there, but it no longer read as self-protection. It had become part of the language. That distinction matters because Pavar’s music is built around control in several senses. She writes, performs, produces and mixes her own material; her arrangements tend towards clarity rather than accumulation; and even live, the electronic architecture necessarily fixes certain parameters in advance. Yet the more interesting development is how she has begun using that control to create freedom rather than insulation. She speaks here about abandoning perfection as a useful measure, learning that a stage persona does not need to be a separate personality, and discovering that authenticity can emerge gradually rather than through some dramatic act of self-reinvention. That makes the timing of this conversation particularly interesting. Her second album, “six”, appeared in March 2025, followed later that year by “REMIXES”, which handed her tightly controlled compositions to artists including Radondo, Kay-Chi, Skelesys, New Haunts and others. In August 2026, “too much” opened another phase: more direct, more emotionally immediate and, in Pavar’s own words, less subtle. Rather than presenting this as a clean break with what came before, she seems more interested in testing how far the existing language can stretch. The final answer she gives here may be the simplest description of that process: think less, be bolder. Rina Pavar interview Karo: I saw you at NCN only a few days ago, on the Parkbühne, and I was thinking about how peculiar the setting actually was for your music: an early festival slot, daylight, people still arriving and adjusting to the day. Does a situation like that require you to construct your own atmosphere almost against the surroundings, or do you prefer not to impose a predetermined mood on a performance at all? Rina: Yes, that was really unusual. But I always take as much time as possible beforehand to rehearse and visualise the specific setting and the audience. I was familiar with NCN and the Parkbühne from a guest’s perspective, so I could easily imagine what my performance would feel and look like at that time. I think this approach allows me to adapt more flexibly to the circumstances, including in my song selection and the style of my performance. Even though, of course, the core always remains the same, the details change with every performance. Karo: When you spoke to Side-Line in 2023, performing was still relatively new territory for you and the studio was very much the place where you felt most secure. Three years later, I watched someone who seemed considerably more settled within the physical act of performing. What changed? Was it simply accumulated experience, or did you have to discover a different version of yourself onstage? Rina: I think it’s a little bit of both. So far, I still don’t approach the unknown entirely without fear or hesitation. That’s why practice and experience remain the cornerstones of my self-confidence and my progress. My stage persona has also changed over time. But through my experiences so far, I’ve realised that there’s actually no need for a “different” version of myself on stage. Rather, as my experience and self-confidence grow, more space opens up for me to enjoy the performance and let my authentic self shine through. That’s why I take the time to discover and refine myself in this environment bit by bit and at my own pace, instead of artificially building something that I’ll eventually have to shed one day because it no longer fits. Karo: “too much” arrived only a few weeks before NCN and has now been presented as the beginning of a new sequence of releases. Why was this particular song the right point of departure? What does it introduce that you felt had not already been said on six? Rina: I think it has a completely different vibe. It’s more direct, more emotional and less subtle in terms of content, without going completely over the top. At least, that’s how I feel about it. That’s why I thought it was the perfect choice for the first single. I’d actually included it in the NCN set, and the reactions were consistently positive. That confirmed my choice. Karo: six contained a great deal of looking backwards: memory, relationships, places, decisions, versions of oneself that have already existed. I wonder whether your writing is changing now from processing experience towards something more immediate. Are you becoming interested in writing from inside an experience while it is still unresolved, rather than only once you understand what it meant? Rina: For me, it always happens in a flexible and spontaneous way. When certain topics or approaches are important to me at the moment, they naturally take centre stage at that time. But things might look completely different again in the next project. Karo: Because you write, perform, produce and mix your own material, almost every important decision remains with you until the mastering stage. That gives you enormous artistic coherence, but presumably also removes the useful resistance another person can provide. How do you recognise the moment when complete creative independence stops being liberating and starts becoming a blind spot? Rina: That’s an important point. And I’ve often had to listen to all the things that can go wrong when you work on your own. That’s why I’ve found the following approach, which works for me. First, I took the pressure off myself to be perfect, and for RINA PAVAR I decided to focus on presenting what comes from me as a person, regardless of whether it’s perfect, good enough, innovative, trendy, cutting-edge or whatever. If it brings me great joy and meets my standards for growth at that moment, then that’s good enough. This creates freedom and keeps me from getting stuck in a safe, rigid framework. Furthermore, with every release, I set new but achievable goals for myself, whether musically, vocally, personally, in live performances or even just in terms of design. I sit down and teach myself something new or try to optimise processes and recognise patterns to eliminate blind spots as much as possible. Karo: There is considerable restraint in your arrangements; individual sounds are often given enough room to become structurally important rather than being surrounded by layers simply because they are available. Is reduction something you consciously work towards? In other words, do you spend as much time deciding what a song can survive without as deciding what it still needs? Rina: I think that’s one of the few things I don’t have to consciously work towards. When I’m producing a song, I actually have to force myself to add elements. I’m always surprised when someone tells me how clean or minimal the mix is. In my mind, I’ve actually “packed it full”, and I often think to myself, “Okay, there’s room for improvement here, and I should be a little bolder in approaching this aspect.” But reduction, or perhaps “clarity” is a better word, is something that runs through everything I do. For me, it’s fulfilling to break down complex situations to their essentials, to distil the core, to organise, structure or simplify things. And that happens completely automatically. Karo: REMIXES placed your songs in the hands of artists with very different instincts, which is almost the opposite of the control you normally have over your work. Was there a remix that revealed something about one of your compositions that you had not recognised yourself, perhaps because another artist emphasised a rhythm, mood or tension that you had considered secondary? Rina: I’d almost say that’s the case with all the songs. Often, my favourite elements are highlighted but placed in a completely different context or emphasised even more. I love every one of these songs and am thrilled to experience my creations in a more developed and reinterpreted form. Karo: Your collaboration with Kay-Chi on “Darkest Night” is interesting for a similar reason, because there you contributed lyrics and vocals to somebody else’s musical framework rather than building the entire environment yourself. Does writing from inside another producer’s world free you in some way, precisely because you are not responsible for every element of the finished piece? Rina: It’s definitely a challenging yet enjoyable situation. I really enjoy not having to take full responsibility for everything. At the same time, though, I often put pressure on myself to do the parts that I work on perfectly. After all, I want to do the song justice and not disappoint the artist who chose me as a collaboration partner. Even though it may seem overwhelming at first, and it’s not always easy to find my place on someone else’s song, I always look forward to projects like this. It’s fun, offers the chance to collaborate and is always a nice change of pace from working solo. Karo: You also work visually, and I am interested less in whether your visual art “matches” the music than in whether the two forms make you think differently. Music unfolds through time, while an image confronts you more or less simultaneously. Does moving between those two ways of organising an idea change the way you compose? Rina: The way I compose doesn’t change because of this. The approaches and the way ideas come to me are simply too different. But painting is my balance to music, and vice versa. For me, it’s a kind of respite from the other and therefore the break I need to develop and bring new ideas to life. Music is often stirring, full of energy and, despite studio work, takes place largely outside. Painting is absolute stillness, tranquillity, grounding and complete isolation from the outside world. Karo: Coldwave and dark electronic music have developed a very recognisable vocabulary, and recognition can become both an advantage and a trap: listeners know immediately where they are, but artists can also end up repeating gestures simply because those gestures belong to the language of the scene. Which elements of that vocabulary still feel central to Rina Pavar, and which ones have you begun questioning? Rina: If I had to name one thing that remains an important, central aspect, or an indispensable element, for me it would be the melancholy in the sound and lyrics. These are still elements of my songs because I’m still drawn to them. But to be honest, I don’t think about genre at all when I’m composing. I create songs based on the premise that “I have to like it” in order to maintain the greatest possible creative freedom. Karo: Electronic performances inevitably contain structures that cannot be altered as freely as they might be in a conventional rock band, yet the person onstage is responding to something entirely unpredictable: an audience. At NCN, how much were you actually reading the people in front of you? Can their response change the way you deliver a song even when its underlying architecture remains fixed? Rina: I can always feel the energy of the audience, and I try to respond to it as best I can. Even though the set is basically fixed, since it’s tied to a tight schedule, especially at a festival like NCN, I still always leave room within that framework to add or omit details, swap out songs, vary my vocal delivery, let loose and adjust the announcements to be longer or shorter depending on how the audience reacts. At NCN, it was great to see that everyone was fully into it even at such an early hour, and that really gave me power. Karo: Your development so far has involved becoming more confident not only as a songwriter but also as someone willing to place herself physically at the centre of the project. At this point, what would artistic growth actually mean to you? Is it greater musical complexity, greater simplicity, taking more emotional risks, collaborating more, reaching larger audiences, or something that has nothing to do with scale at all? Rina: I want to continue acquiring new technical skills and incorporating them into my compositions. When performing live, I’d like to experiment a bit more, both in terms of the performance and the look, as well as the instrumentation. It’s basically a matter of fine-tuning every aspect to bring out and strengthen the essence of RINA PAVAR even more. Karo: Finally, looking ahead: “too much” has been announced as the first of a series of new releases, so we clearly are not looking at an isolated single. Without asking you to reveal anything that should remain a surprise, what is beginning now for Rina Pavar? And when we eventually look back at this next body of work, what do you hope we will hear in it that was not there before? Rina: I do have an idea of what the “new” element will be in the upcoming releases. But since I’m always worried that listeners might not even notice it, I’d like to start by summarising it this way: Think less, be bolder. About Rina Pavar Rina Pavar is a Leipzig-based German solo project started in 2019. Her own Bandcamp describes the music as coldwave and dark electronic music, while Cold Transmission characterises the project through driving basslines, vintage synthesizers, accented vocals and lyrics concerned with consciousness and personal experience. Her debut album, “vivid night”, was released digitally on 1 November 2021, followed by the EP “things we hide” in May 2022. Pavar writes, performs, produces and mixes her own material; those credits are documented on both “vivid night” and her second album. The second album, “six”, was released through Cold Transmission on 21 March 2025. It contains nine tracks and was mastered by Frithjof Rödel at Atomino Studio, with artwork and cover by Pavar and photography by yules_pictures. On 5 December 2025, she released “REMIXES”, a ten-track collection featuring reinterpretations by Radondo, Kay-Chi, Zee Mon, Skelesys, Close Proximity, PJ, Sun’s Spectrum, New Haunts and Three Days Awake by Bent, alongside Pavar’s own club mix of “structured fall”. Pavar also contributed lyrics and vocals to Kay-Chi’s “Darkest Night”, released as part of the Night Protocol EP on 27 March 2026. Her latest single, “too much”, was released on 14 August 2026. Cold Transmission announced it as the first in a series of new releases, marking the beginning of the next phase of the project.
items._cn_summary: Rina Pavar 集词曲、演奏、后期制作为一体，创作以精准的控制为核心，电子架构构成了声音的骨架。她的第二张专辑《six》于2025年3月发行，展现了清晰的编曲逻辑；同年问世的《REMIXES》将作品交由Radondo、Kay-Chi、Skelesys等艺人重构。2026年的《too much》标志着风格的转变，从含蓄内敛转向更为直接与情感外露的表达。她在专访中谈到放弃完美主义作为衡量标准，意识到舞台形象不必与本人割裂，真诚可以逐步建立而非通过戏剧化的自我重塑来实现。整体来看，这是一位独立艺术家对自身音乐语言的渐进式拓展——通过保留核心结构来测试表达的边界，最终归纳为'少想，更大胆'的创作态度。

items.body: Oh, holding on to yon and bitter falter Endless yearning weaves its web Among the forest, sheltered by her alter To be free, to be free Society of the Silver Cross draws on Gothic music’s old appetite for grand architecture, spiritual unease, and whatever might lie beyond ordinary daylight. Joe Reineke and Karyn Gold-Reineke built Temple of the Trees in Seattle, in part to accommodate that vision, filling the place with instruments that make a person wonder whether somebody has opened an archaeological dig beneath the control room. Their ongoing Temple Hymns series turns that studio into a meeting ground. Each installment brings another musician into the room to write and record with the pair, allowing personality, instinct, and whatever strange chemistry develops over several concentrated days to determine the results. Volume One brought in T.J. Cowgill of King Dude. For Temple Hymns Volume Two, Blood and Sun founder Luke Tromiczak flew from New York to Seattle and spent a week working with Reineke and Gold-Reineke. Tromiczak has led Blood and Sun since 2011, developing one of neofolk’s most recognizable baritones along the way. Put that voice beside twelve-string acoustic guitar, harmonium, B3 organ, Shahi Baaja, obscure synthesizers, and great booming toms and suddenly the room starts feeling considerably older than Seattle. Blood and Sun founder Luke Tromiczak Unraveled moves at the pace of somebody following a mountain trail after sunset with complete confidence that something significant waits at the other end. Its language circles freedom, transformation, lunar power, broken mirrors, concealed paths, and the promise of reunion. The arrangement carries the stateliness of Leonard Cohen into territory closer to Rowland S. Howard, while those deep drums suggest Ennio Morricone scoring some outlaw procession whose participants have traded revolvers for incense. The repetition in the vocal becomes nearly chant-like, working against the twelve-string guitar and organ until the track takes on a devotional character. Indian musical influence sits naturally beside American folk forms, giving the song an unusual spiritual geography. You can hear bits of Nick Cave, Nero Kane, and the Gun Club somewhere along the road, though everything has been dragged far enough into the Silver Cross universe to lose its passport. Battled Hands feels earthier, wounded by experience yet stubbornly pointed toward recovery in a call and response ballad. Tromiczak sings about endurance with the authority of somebody who understands that survival rarely comes accompanied by trumpets. Fire, dawn, damaged hands, storms, mercy, and returning light become markers along a long recovery from suffering. The slow progression allows each image enough room to settle before the drums push forward again. There is something almost physical about the weight of Tromiczak’s voice against the instrumentation. Reineke and Gold-Reineke surround him with enough space for every low note to feel carved into the room, while the harmonium and organ carry the devotional aspect further without turning the song into meaningless ceremony. Together, these two pieces make Temple Hymns Volume Two into a record of musicians discovering exactly how much ground they share. Listen to Temple Hymns Volume Two and order the double single here. Temple Hymns Vol. 2 by Society of the Silver Cross & Blood and Sun Society of the Silver Cross and Blood and Sun will take that meeting across Europe next month, where these songs should sound perfectly comfortable inside clubs, cellars, old halls, and any room willing to surrender its ordinary dimensions for a few minutes. items.body: I’m a living god In the same way as all human flesh A pretty song can pose a problem when your band has spent a decade cultivating less agreeable habits. Melbourne quartet Bitumen found themselves facing precisely that predicament with “Perffect Dress,” a handful of chords that had begun behaving suspiciously well. Their response was to introduce a little trouble: vocal distortion, an outlaw-country inflection, and a bouzouki. Beauty survived the intervention, though its manners became considerably less predictable. The single offers an unexpected turn ahead of Reality Red, the band’s third album, due November 6 via It Records. Acoustic instruments and live drums open up fresh possibilities for a group whose post-punk has long accommodated goth, metal, and electronic abrasion. Here, that expansion takes the form of something loose-limbed and oddly pastoral, with a threat tucked into its Sunday best. A slow drum crash and twanging acoustic guitar set the pace, with further strings gathering around the opening figure. There is a country-folk lilt to the arrangement, carried by the easy movement of Andrew Huhtanen McEwan’s drums and Bryce Maher’s bouzouki. As the layers accumulate, a deep bass hum draws the music toward alternative rock and post-punk, while a high electric-guitar line swims through the spaces overhead. The song seems happy to wander, even as its low end keeps track of where everyone is going. Kate Binning’s voice gives that wandering its peculiar charm. Her vocal suggests Marianne Faithfull meets Thom Yorke’s languid reverie. The distortion adds texture without making the performance abrasive; there is an almost whimsical quality to the delivery, a daydream being sung aloud before anyone has checked its contents. Simon Maisch’s murmured backing vocals move beneath her, introducing a second, less easily deciphered train of thought. The words supply ample reason to inspect that daydream. Revenge, freeway exposure, pursuit, and the vulnerability of flesh run through lyrics that keep shifting between smallness and grandiosity. The speaker can be a little sound one moment and a living god the next, claiming divinity on the same terms as every other mortal body. Rearranging a perfect dress becomes a wonderfully incongruous gesture amid all this damage: a small adjustment to one’s appearance while existence itself appears to be coming apart. The overlapping vocal lines complicate the picture further, slipping bodily images and cryptic instructions beneath the lead. The accompanying video places the band around an open fire against corrugated metal, their faces and instruments catching its orange light. Rectangular close-ups overlap the wider performance, bringing hands on strings and Binning’s singing face into the foreground while the gathering continues behind them. As those frames change size and position, the clip moves between collective intimacy and private concentration. It suits the song’s peculiar hospitality: pull up a chair, enjoy the acoustic guitars, and try to overlook the revenge being discussed beside the flames. Watch the video for Perffect Dress below: ﻿ Formed in Melbourne in 2016, Bitumen brings together Kate Binning, Sam Varney, Bryce Maher, and Simon Maisch. Working with a drum machine has been a deliberate part of their approach, allowing guitars, synthesizers, samples, and programmed rhythms to change the terms of each song. On Reality Red, Tongue Dissolver’s McEwan adds live drums to that existing setup, while acoustic instrumentation and a greater openness to melody give the four-piece further room to experiment. Perffect Dress was recorded by Maisch at Lily Street Studios in Coburg North, with McEwan assisting, and produced by the band. Reality Red is available to pre-order here on digital and limited-edition transparent red vinyl through It Records. items._cn_summary: 墨尔本四人组Bitumen在单曲《Perffect Dress》中打破以往棱角分明的后朋克惯例，引入原声吉他、布祖基琴和略带乡村色彩的节奏，同时保留失真人声与低音嗡鸣带来的暗潮式张力。歌曲在松散牧歌般的律动中暗藏威胁感，Kate Binning的人声兼具Marianne Faithfull的沉静与Thom Yorke的慵懒，Simon Maisch的低语和声在底层编织出第二条叙事线索。歌词在渺小与神性之间反复切换，涉及报复、公路追逐、肉体脆弱等意象。配套MV以篝火与波纹金属为背景，矩形特写与群像交替，呼应歌曲既邀请又疏离的氛围。这首单曲为11月6日发行的第三张专辑《Reality Red》预告，展示了乐队在后朋克框架内对原声乐器与田野质感的探索。

items.body: I didn't really like Holocene. I could, however, appreciate it. That distinction is important: while the album wasn't for me, I could see what The Ocean were trying to do with it. More than that, I accepted that experimentation and change was the entire point of the project. Hell, Pelagial (still my favorite album from the band) is built around the very idea of change and transformation. But the direction the band was going in wasn't for me; I didn't think they executed it with enough skill to hold my interest. And so, I approached Solaris with some trepidation. I knew what to expect, namely something different, especially when I heard that four new band members were being added. What form would The Ocean take this time? Would some of the "old" sound return and, more importantly I think, did I want it to?Well, the answer to both of those questions is "sort of". Solaris is definitely more akin to Pelagial and Phanerozoic than Holocene was. It has plenty of electronic sounds and touches to it but it very much revolves around some of the tried and true elements of The Ocean, namely post-metal built around a concept album. But there are also differences. As you might be able to tell from looking at the cover art, Solaris is a "brighter" album. What do I mean by that? First, the compositions are less organized around crushing force and more around exploration and melody. Even Phanerozoic, which wasn't explicitly built around the concept of weight like Pelagial was, used its instruments to oppress and crush. But Solaris has a whole gamut of new sounds; check out "Light Pollution" for example and the undulating, mercurial segment around the four minute mark and especially the exquisite guitar bridge around four minutes and fifty seconds.Have you really heard The Ocean do this in the past? Not quite. And while you're there, you probably picked up on the vocals of Lane Shi (Elizabeth Color Wheel, Fórn) who is by far the biggest new addition to this album. The Loic Rosetti style vocals, which Enrico Tiberi does an uncanny job of recreating, really benefit from having a counter-part on this release. It's not that Tiberi's voice is boring. But the interaction between his timbre and the rest of The Ocean's instruments is tried and true. Shi, on the other hand, brings a whole new texture and palette to the record, creating much of that "brightness" I was referring to earlier. Whether screaming, vocalizing, humming, or emoting she's a breath of fresh air to the record and my favorite change on it by far. Other changes include those I've already highlighted, like new ideas from new guitarists, new ideas for how tracks are "stitched" together, like the bells on "Simulacra" or the overall approach to leitmotifs and guitar riffs on the album.Speaking about "Simulacra", holy shit do I love this track. It's perhaps my favorit example of what Solaris does so well. It's definitely The Ocean but it also sounds so different, the chords chosen, the structure of the track, the synths, even what Staps does with his singing on this track. It builds up to something much more exciting than just a retread. Rather, it's a rethink, an approach to the band's past that insists not just on regurgitation but a reprocessing that results in a new approach towards the same goal and sound. Which brings me back to the question of did I want the "old" The Ocean back and my answer of "sort of". I am very happy to hear the heaviness come back to the foreground and The Ocean back to what they do well: creating meticulously constructed, concept heavy post-metal. But I am also equally happy that they did not go back to Pelagial or Phanerozoic, as much as I love those releases. I am extremely glad that they held on to what I think makes them unique and yes, what sometimes leads them to make releases I don't enjoy as much: their fierce dedication to change. You never know what The Ocean will do next and they have proven this once again on Solaris. Thankfully, the end result is also something I love.
items._genre: post-metal / experimental rock / progressive / electronic-infused metal
items._cn_summary: The Ocean 的新专辑《Solaris》延续其概念专辑传统，在后金属框架内融入更多电子音色与旋律化探索。相比前作《Holocene》，本作色调更明亮，弱化了压迫性的重量感，转而强调旋律铺陈与器乐实验。新成员吉他手带来新思路，人声方面加入了 Lane Shi 的女性声线，与原有 Enrico Tiberi 的演绎形成丰富互动。电子元素的运用更为克制但精准，如铃声、导动机、合成器质感的段落在《Simulacra》《Light Pollution》中提供层次感。整体在保持乐队辨识度的同时拓展了声景边界，概念执行与情绪变化之间取得平衡，是一支在后金属基础上持续自我更新的作品。

items.body: These original soundscapes – from anthéne, Slow Dancing Society, and orchestramaxfieldparrish – are a tribute to Joni Mitchell. Swallowed by the Sky, textura’s fourth release, is a homage to the singer-songwriter, revealing a deep appreciation for both person and music. Her legacy stretches far beyond any one genre or style, and while these aren’t covers – far from it – they channel her spirit. In some ways, they come closer to the truth of her music, touching meanings and lighting upon atmospheres in a deeper way. Covers can’t replicate that. While there are plenty of compilations and covers of her songs, there hasn’t been much, if anything, in the way of ambient. Such is her range, she’s inspired artists and musicians from all over the musical spectrum, going way into other stylistic fields and touching all different areas of music. Just as Jeff Stonehouse channelled the spirit of Mexico’s Chavela Vargas with his Listening Mirror release, On The Passing of Chavela, so too do these three ambient musicians dedicate their music to Joni, and in doing so, they evoke something just as deep as her soulful songs. This sweet, soothing music has a light, feminine touch, singing on the air like a wordless expression of her vocal poetry. Lyrics are huge in popular music, but music is so much more than that, and these instrumentals are able to delicately touch wider borders without the sweet entanglement of vocals. Brad Deschamps, Drew Sullivan, and Mike Fazio are all under her spell, and the music demonstrates a deep admiration and respect. The pieces also explore the light-and-dark juxtapositions in her songs. Lightness is eclipsed and replaced by a subtle change in mood, the sky becoming overcast and sullen; a changing of the times. The bass is an anchor, and melodies are allowed to blossom: the trio give their pieces sustenance and grounding, and, much like Joni’s songs, they come from a place deep down in the soul, given free roam to flower. SWALLOWED BY THE SKY by anthéne | Slow Dancing Society | orchestramaxfieldparrish www.textura.bandcamp.com
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑由三位氛围音乐人共同创作，向歌手Joni Mitchell致敬。三位艺术家分别以环境音乐质感重新诠释她的音乐精神，将原本以人声歌词为核心的作品转化为纯器乐的声景，触及原作更深层的情绪氛围。专辑并非简单翻唱，而是通过绵密的低频锚点与缓慢展开的旋律线条，捕捉原作中光影交织的情绪变化——明亮与阴暗的交替如同天空中云层聚散。整体音乐柔和而细腻，如同无言的声诗，漂浮于空中。低音为作品提供沉稳根基，旋律在其上自然绽放，展现出对Joni Mitchell音乐遗产的深度理解与敬意。作为独立小厂牌Textura的第四张发行物，这种跨类型的致敬方式——将民谣精神转化为氛围音景——展现了一种独特而内敛的创作思路。

items.body: Sudan Dudan is a Norwegian duo, Marit Karlberg and Anders Erik R�ine, who have released four albums over the last twenty years. On M�rke refrenger , their fifth, they are joined by Hans Hulb�kmo and Magnus Skavhaug Nergaard, contributing instrumentally and with the production. There are eight songs on the album with accompaniment principally led by acoustic guitar, augmented by fiddles, langeleik, lyre, jaws harp and more. The opening track, �Gard og grind� (�Fence and gate�) is a fine introduction to what is to come: finger-picked acoustic guitar, fiddle, bass and snare-drum played with brushes leading into the harmonized vocal, together creating an alluring sound drawing the listener in. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The mood of the album, reflected in its title which translates as �Dark Refrains,� is not always dark, but most of the material, including the title track, certainly has a reflective quality. According to the press release �the lyrics smoulder with unease about the present and the future, while looking back to the myths and riddles of the past. They speak of the earth, the sun, the moon, stars and planets, of lost brothers, quarrelling sisters, loss and grief, of the power of imagination, and of the answers to the simplest and most difficult riddles.� The lyrics of all the songs, in Norwegian, are included in the sleeve notes and while a hasty online translation can aid with some understanding, the full meanings tend to remain cryptic, but there is a sense that words and music complement each other. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan For all its dark moodiness, M�rke refrenger does have its lighter moments. �Bagatelle� recalls and reinvents the melody of a well-known French song, adding some off-kilter harmonies, while �Rulleball� is more characteristically Norwegian, employing a vocal style known as tralling in which words are replaced by a vocalization of the melody, originally used to accompany dances when no instrument was available. No translation necessary there. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The final track �Skriften p� veggen� (�the writing on the wall�) features, for the only time on the album, electric guitar. The sound is deep and twangy, shades of Duane Eddy or a David Lynch soundtrack and it works very well. All in all a fine, imaginatively conceived and beautifully produced record, available as a download or vinyl. Find the artists online. items.body:
According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

items.body:
A debut, digital-only EP from a Danish trio, led by one of the Nordic folk scene�s outstanding and experienced vocalists, Mia Guldhammer. Five tracks, with the musicians bringing their own perspectives to mostly traditional music. There�s a lovely ancient, creaky mood throughout.
The opener, �Svennedal,� with its rough, cantering rhythm, offers a perfect shop window for Guldhammer�s impressive, persuasive voice, while jaw harp and bagpipes bring an insistent propulsion to �Nordg�rd,� the only original here, by band member Morten Musicus.
Cimbalom adds a delicate backdrop to the traditional �Agnete Of Bjergmanden,� with Guldhammer�s soft jaw harp offering extra textures to the other instruments, as it brings a springy opening to the final cut, �Orms�,� mingling with flute and strings to create something quite thrilling and off kilter on this instrumental.
Five tracks, and an introduction to a band that already seems very mature and accomplished. A strong beginning � what will GuldGanger do with an entire album?

items._cn_summary: 这是丹麦三人组合GuldGanger的首张数字EP，五首曲目以传统北欧民谣为底色。主唱Mia Guldhammer是北欧民谣圈内经验丰富的实力派歌手，其浑厚且具说服力的嗓音贯穿全片。专辑在编制上呈现丰富的传统乐器层次：簧风琴、风笛、扬琴、长笛与弦乐交织，营造出古旧、略带粗粝的氛围。开场曲《Svennedal》以粗犷的奔跑节奏展开，唯一原创曲《Nordgård》由成员Morten Musicus贡献，簧风琴与风笛推动全曲前行。传统曲目《Agnete Of Bjergmanden》中扬琴铺设精致底色，器乐曲《Orms》融合长笛与弦乐产生不安分的弹性律动。作为一支首张作品，乐队展现出超出预期的成熟度，为后续全长专辑留下期待空间。

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — Vitelli has always had a well-stocked address book, including even a few living legends of '70s prog (Anthony Phillips, Tony Pagliuca, and David Cross, to name just a few, have contributed to Ellesmere's previous albums). This even allowed him to bring together no fewer than five exceptional guitarists in 2018 for *From Sea And Beyond* (Alan Benjamin, Trey Gunn, Keith More, Davy O'List, and Brett Kull, no less). On *Stranger Skies*, the lineup of prestigious guests continues. Surrounding the core lineup of Vitelli on bass and keyboards, Giacomo Anselmi (Goblin Rebirth) on electric guitars, Stefano Vicarelli (Fonderia) on Moog and Mellotron, and Mattias Olsson (who needs no introduction)?a master of odd time signatures and off-beat rhythms, who once again brings his crisp, precise, and creative drumming, the band brings together a few musicians?whom, like Olsson, we're tempted to leave unintroduced?including figures from prog of yesterday and today (Clive Nolan, Tomas Bodin, Riccardo Romano), well-known veterans (John Hackett, David Jackson), and others less so, such as Graeme Taylor (one of Gryphon's leaders) or Bob Hodges (Czar).Ellesmere's previous albums were mostly instrumental, featuring occasional guest vocalists (we recall Robert Berry's performance on *From Sea And Beyond*, though perhaps less so that of Luciano Regoli, the leader of Raccomandata Ricevuta Ritorno, an old RPI band) Here, it's the opposite: one and the same voice throughout, that of the remarkable and much-talked-about John Wilkinson. As the lead singer of the Liverpool band The Swan Chorus (with two albums to their credit, one released in 2018 and the other in 2023) and a member of Mama?which, as its name suggests, is a band that covers songs from Genesis's Phil Collins era?John brings a vocal tone so close to Collins's that it's almost uncanny. John Wilkinson can also be heard on a few tracks from the recent Samurai of Prog releases, such as "Like An Endless Sea" from Bernard & P�rsti's *Robinson Crusoe*.With the relative resurgence of the vinyl market offering an opportunity to make a little extra money, some progressive artists don't hesitate to shorten the length of their CDs and organize them into Side A and Side B, with an eye toward a potential vinyl release. Recently, the Canadian band Monarch Trail even titled their new album *Four Sides*, clearly signaling their intention to present it as a double album in the spirit of the golden age of the LP. Similarly, the first four tracks (totaling 23 minutes) of *Stranger Skies* are described as the "cold side" (meaning the more rock-oriented section), and the last two tracks?which are longer (totaling 24 minutes)?as the "hot side" (meaning more progressive). We'll see that it's not quite that simple.At the risk of sounding pedantic, let's dive right in with a track-by-track walkthrough of the album. Track #1, the first on Side A, known as the "cold" side: "Northwards" (6:50). After a majestic introduction in the classical symphonic style featuring Clive Nolan's keyboards, Ellesmere manages to revive?by blending them?the styles that Yes and Genesis had more or less adopted around 1977 (specifically, the tracks "Going For The One" and "Down And Out" as references): a multitrack sound, rich in effects and reverb, and a warm, full-bodied voice saturated with echo. Track #2: "Tundra" (6:43). Closer to early '80s Rush, especially in the chord arpeggios of a martial keyboard and the plump bass line characteristic of the Canadian band (it's no coincidence, by the way, that Vitelli's four-string Fender is named "Geddy Lee"!). A breathtaking fusion guitar solo closes out "Tundra" in the epic style of Dave Bainbridge. Track #3: "Crystallized," the only instrumental. In the intro, performed by Taylor, we catch a glimpse of the "Anthony Philips-style acoustic-pastoral" state of grace from the first album. It's a refreshing and welcome breather amid these intense three-quarters of an hour, with no downtime or let-up?which, paradoxically, might be the only criticism one could level at this album, provided you enjoy symphonic prog with unapologetic grandeur. The next track, a powerful neo-prog piece enhanced by David Jackson's unrestrained saxophone?which adds prog-fusion colors?is more in line with the rest of the album. Track #4: "Arctica" (4:16). The influence of Rush returns, with just as much energy and conviction but without the melodic clarity of the Toronto trio. A slight weak spot on *Stranger Skies*, despite the strength of the performance.Track #5, the first on Side B, known as the "hot" side: "Stranger Skies" (12:17). Closer to Steve Hackett's recent solo albums?his brother is once again on flute here?and less "edgy" than on *Wyrd*. John's vocals naturally seem to draw closer to those of Nad Sylvan. Along the way, one is also reminded of BBT or the most prog-oriented moments of Phil Collins' solo career. Track #6: "Another World" (11:43). We head in the direction of Arena, with Genesis from '78?'80 still in mind, particularly Rutherford's compositions. The final three minutes mark a complete break. Graceful and subtle, exquisite and imaginative, this finale?performed with delicacy by Tomas Bodin, which becomes obvious upon listening?is a lovely coda that stands in stark contrast to everything that came before.With musical themes more captivating than ever, greater cohesion than before, a consistent density that doesn't preclude fluidity, high-quality vocals, and a style a world away from the first album?closer to the subsequent ones while correcting their weaknesses or missteps but retaining their beautiful generosity? *Stranger Skies* is the most captivating of Roberto Vitelli's albums released under the name Ellesmere.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由意大利制作人 Vitelli 主导的 Ellesmere 项目出品，围绕贝斯与键盘核心，召集了 Goblin Rebirth、Fonderia 等乐队成员及多位横跨七十年代至今的前卫摇滚客座乐手。乐队延续了前几张作品邀请传奇人物参与的传统，本辑统一由嗓音酷似 Phil Collins 的 John Wilkinson 担任主唱，取代以往器乐为主的模式。专辑被设计为黑胶两面的结构：前四轨被定位为偏摇滚的"冷面"，后两轨共二十四分钟则是更前卫的"热面"。Mattias Olsson 的鼓击以清晰精准和复杂节拍著称，Moog 与 Mellotron 的加入强化了交响前卫的色彩。整体属于典型的复古学院派交响前卫路线，对资深 Prog 听众有较强吸引力，但在声音实验与跨界融合方面较为保守。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Logos channels a classic Gothic symphonic rock sound; the use of synthesizers and keyboards in "Origami in SOL" serves as an introduction to a complex musical tapestry reminiscent of Metamorfosi, particularly in "Paesaggi di insonnia," a track that borders on psychedelia through its juxtaposition of keyboard layers. The spirit of Genesis, combined with the saxophone, creates a dense atmosphere that nonetheless flows effortlessly, thanks to a dark, epic jazz influence, driven by a powerful underlying purpose: this is a concept album about the life of Sadako Sasaki. She was a Japanese girl who was two years old at the time of the nuclear attack on Hiroshima; she later fell ill and passed away at the age of twelve. This story gave rise to the Japanese legend of the thousand paper cranes (origami) that Sadako attempted to fold in the hope of recovering.The track's frenetic pace in Un lieto inquietarsi, is comparable to Le Orme's magnum opus, Felona e Sorona; the interplay between the drums, keyboards, and synthesizer weaves a musical tapestry that sets the stage for various solos, while an ominous aura gradually takes hold, including a decidedly non-festive use of the Hammond organ.Shifts in tempo occur naturally, amidst the abruptness with which the music bursts forth, drawing upon the full majesty of the classical repertoire, where Baroque polyphony paves the way for Luca Zerman's vocals, which adapt seamlessly to the context. In Il Sarto one notices the resemblance of Luca Zerman's voice to Aldo Tagliapietra (from Le Orme) and then he is joined by Elisa Montaldo, pianist and singer of the progressive band Il Tempio Delle Clessidre, in a great and emotional duet."Zaini di Elio" begins with the feel of 1970s Genesis, specifically the Phil Collins era, before allowing itself to be captivated by the structures of J.S. Bach; combined with Alessandro Perbellini's drumming, the music takes on the quality of a dance alongside the electric clavichord. It evokes Tony Banks and Phil Collins during the ...And Then There Were Three... period, though the sound drifts toward a more pastoral atmosphere, incorporating traditional vocal elements from the artist's native Verona. The layering of the various keyboard lines is so delicate that the transitions are imperceptible: it sounds as though the music had always been there.Sadako e le mille gru di cartareminds me of Hiroshima Mon Amour, Alain Resnais's film, and the subtlety of addressing such a subject with poetry and respect; stepping back to draw closer from a different angle, the kind of perspective only the passage of time can provide. Here, Claudio Antolini's piano takes on a new depth, and the rhythm that has driven the album pauses. Musical passages evoke Eastern melodies, telling the story through sound, accompanied by ghostly-sounding Minimoog emulations. Never before has a folded sheet, a crumpled scrap of paper, held so many layers of meaning or interpretation. The music provides the accompaniment: dramatic, yet also epic and inspiring, conveying a strength that rises from the ashes. Driven by keyboards and drums, the composition blends classical elements with syncopated rhythms, building toward an operatic finale as the paper figure unfolds, a symbol of the hope that nothing happens in vain, even if it seems otherwise at the time. That was precisely the hidden meaning behind the twists and intersections of the music itself.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以日本真实人物佐佐木禎子的生平为概念主题，讲述广岛核爆幸存者在生命最后阶段折叠千纸鹤的故事。音乐以意大利前卫摇滚传统为基础，大量运用合成器、键盘层叠与哈蒙德管风琴，营造哥特式的浓郁氛围，同时融入巴洛克复调与东方旋律元素。乐队在器乐编排上展现出明显的70年代Genesis与Le Orme印记，速度转换自然，鼓、键盘与合成器之间的交织构成密集的织体。专辑还引入爵士管乐与明诺合成器音色，钢琴段落被赋予东方式的叙事空间。歌词以诗意而非直白的方式处理沉重题材，呼应阿兰·雷乃电影《广岛之恋》那种以时间距离回望历史的克制美学。

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — For the most part early 70s German Krautrock morphed into the more instrumentally demanding Krautjazz fusion that found a rather sizable following in the second half of the decade when prog ingeneral had declined. Some bands though found a nice middle ground between the heady koschmischevibes of the space age and placed them alongside the more focused workouts of the jazz fusion scene.One such band was MORPHEUS that was spawned from an earlier band called Opossum which existed from1971 to 1975 but was never successful at releasing its own material although an archival releasewould see the light of day decades later in 2003. While Opossum was a more free form jazz kinda Kraut, a couple members wanted to play more psych-soaked structured tracks in the vein of other German fusion acts such as Kraan and Missus Beastleyor Embryo for that matter. The results was the short-lived MORPHEUS from Warburg that existed fortwo years from 1975 to 1977 and released its one and only album RABENTEUER smack dab in the middleof its career in 1976. Far from free form, MORPHEUS gathered grooves from the world of prog rock,trippy effects from the Kraut scene and more accessible jazz stylings also from the German scene.The result was a nicely displayed album that rocked, was smothered in jazz and offered a moresubdued heady vibe courtesy of spacey effects and a sensual flautist on board.Another of the many rarities that were generated during the era, RABENTEUER was limited to 500copies and went undiscovered until the Garden of Delights label resurrected the album for a 1998 CDrelease. Steeped in psych-fueled jazz rock, RABENTEUER features six all-instrumental tracks thatoffer funk-fueled bass grooves, gnarled workouts that offer labyrinthine structured compositions toflow around a rather accessible compositional flair only fortified with complex soundscapes,bountiful helpings of time signature deviations and ample doses of soloing between the variousmusicians that consisted of Peter Bl�meke (bass, flute), Gerold Adler (guitar), Heinrich Holtgreve(alto saxophone) and Alfred Franke (drums). While the tracks are primarily upbeat and more in thejazz rock camp, "Tanz Der Morphine" takes a dive into the space rock world of koschmische Kraut.Like many of the similarly minded bands of the era, MORPHEUS delivered the chops as far as jazz-infused prog was concerned with nice accessible hooks augmented by the more complex attributes ofthe words of both prog and fusion however the album as competently performed as it is sounds a bitlike those same similarly minded acts that didn't really add a lot to the world of jazz fusion atthis stage in the game. The tracks are pleasant but almost by the books in approach without any realfiery passion emerging by the rather consistent display of instrumental interplay. Overall it's anice supplemental piece from the era but not one that strikes me as utterly essential either.Pleasant but not much else. The CD version offers an extra long 20-minute jam track but this is evenof less interest than the album in general.3.5 rounded down
items._cn_summary: 1976年德国乐队MORPHEUS的唯一专辑，源自前身Opossum，融合了Krautrock的太空迷幻氛围、爵士融合的器乐编排以及前卫摇滚的复杂结构。六首纯器乐作品以贝斯主导的放克律动为基础，穿插迷宫式作曲架构、频繁的拍号变化与即兴solo，长笛与萨克管的运用带来感官化的空间质感，其中'Tanz Der Morphine'偏向宇宙摇滚方向。评论者指出乐队演奏技术合格，旋律易记且融合层次丰富，但在风格上与同时期的Kraan、Embryo等德语融合乐队并无显著差异，缺乏突破性的个人标识，整体属于'合格但非必需'的补充之作。该专辑仅限量500张，1998年由Garden of Delights再版CD。

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — Sometimes a rest is as good as a change. Having disbanded after the underwhelming "Lantaloon", DANDO SHAFT resurfaced for one 1977 album with all the principals still available, though Polly doesn't sing any lead at all and is almost just there for the credits. In the meantime, a few dignitaries help expand the credit list, namely ROD CLEMENTS of LINDISFARNE and DANNY THOMPSON of PENTANGLE both on bass, as well as a fledgling saxophonist Paul Dunmall who usurps the spotlight whether it's on him or not. But is it prog? And is it good? Yes. It's that rare comeback album from the late 1970s that pleasantly surprises. It asks the "what if" question or makes the "if only" statement , in this case, could this have changed the bands fortunes if released in 1973? The rock component, notably the bluesy electric guitars and percussions, are just one aspect that elevates this above DANDO's usual twee personae, with the violins fitting like a fiddle, illuminating the mastery of "Follow You", perhaps the group's best track, and "Feel Like I wanna go home". "Trees" marks the return of the olde Englishe and Celtic credentials, even more formidably on the sophisticated "Lady and Man", If it weren't for the preponderance of average albeit absolutely competent numbers, I could give this a roundup, but it's still a miniature triumph worthy of highness if not majesty.
items._cn_summary: 这是英国民谣组合在沉寂多年后的回归之作，1977年发行。专辑在保留民谣根基的同时大胆融入了电吉他、打击乐和萨克斯风，Paul Dunmall的萨克斯成为亮点，与小提琴形成独特对话。Rod Clements和Danny Thompson等嘉宾贝斯手的加入丰富了低音声部。曲目在英式民谣与凯尔特传统之间游走，部分作品展现了乐队少有的摇滚力量感，编曲层次分明。小提琴的运用是专辑的核心特色，既能烘托民谣氛围，也能在摇滚段落中提供有力的旋律支撑。然而专辑整体仍以传统民谣框架为主，实验性有限，虽有亮点却未达到真正意义上的跨界突破。

items.body: Review by greenpete — They made a startlingly confident beginning with their exuberant, minor-label debut, An Evening With Dando Shaft (no, not a live album). But Dando Shaft's high-water mark arrived with this, their sophomore LP (often called the "Carousel" album, and released on RCA's short-lived Neon label, which only issued 11 albums total). This record dispenses entirely with drums, plunging deeper into varied, lyrical progressive folk. Singer Polly Bolton, from the wonderfully named village of Leamington Spa, joined the boys to bolster their string intricacies with her breathy, Sandy Denny-esque voice. The debut was marred only by the awkward "The Cat Song," but on the Carousel album, there's really not a bad cut. The Bulgarian-rhythmic songs of dual guitarists Dave Cooper and Kevin Dempsey, and mega-instrumentalist Martin Jenkins, are consistently strong, with Jenkins' mandolin, flute, and fiddle shining here. His tune "Whispering Ned," about a gent who enjoys indulging in sugar cubes (and whom the band evidently knew) adds an imaginative twist to the canon of drug songs. The upbeat "Pass it On" is notable for its exuberant chorus about values that have, sadly, since gone out of style. But the real highlights are "Till the Morning Comes" and "River Boat." Both feature Bolton's angelic vocals, the former a wispy duet with Cooper graced by luscious, gently psychedelic flute (Jenkins) and tablas (Ted Kay); and the latter an utterly breathtaking, pastoral delight that conjures green, rural England in poem-song.Bolton would stick around for Lantaloon, a good but inessential album, then depart after tiring of feeling like a "guest" vocalist. So if you plan to only get one album by this highly underappreciated psych-folk band...take a ride on the Carousel.- greenpete
items._cn_summary: Dando Shaft 的第二张专辑完全摒弃了鼓的运用，深入探索抒情化的前卫民谣路径。吉他双人组 Dave Cooper 与 Kevin Dempsey 带来保加利亚节奏风格的弹拨，多乐器手 Martin Jenkins 的曼陀林、长笛与小提琴在编曲中占据重要位置。歌手 Polly Bolton 以近似 Sandy Denny 的空灵声线为弦乐编织增添人声层次，其与 Cooper 在《Till the Morning Comes》中的轻盈对唱配合 Jenkins 的迷幻长笛与 Ted Kay 的塔布拉鼓，呈现出东西方乐器融合的细腻质感。《River Boat》则是一首田园牧歌式的作品，以诗歌化的旋律勾勒出英格兰乡村的绿色图景。专辑整体延续英国民谣传统，同时融入保加利亚节奏元素与印度打击乐器，体现了民谣音乐在地域融合上的早期探索。作为英国独立厂牌 Neon 旗下仅有的十一部发行之一，其稀缺性也增加了收藏价值。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Early (First Wave) Jazz-Rock from Poland. This band's debut, we find them experimenting with blending several styles including Blues-Rock, Psychedelia, Procol Harum-like prog, orchestra-enriched lounge music, and more. The album was released in 1971 by Polskie Nagrania Muza.1. "Sen (A Dream)" (3:17) what feels like an ANTHONY PHILLIPS guitar piece opens this for the first 1:07 before a pause unleashes a bouncing organ chord, funky bass line, and Michael Giles-like drumming with simplistic guitar riffs over the top to announce the presence of melody. In the final 30 seconds there is this all out burst of WHO-like energy being expressed/expelled by all of the band members--which then seems to bleed/lead into the SANTANA-like frenzy that is the next song. A three-part suite in three minutes! Wow! (9.333/10)2. "Kuszenie (Temptation)" (3:29) the SANTANA-like percussion-driven full-band jam that features everybody flying at full speed. Maciej Gluszkiewicz' organ impresses as do the performances of all of the quartet members. (9.25/10)3. "Nerwy Miasta (The Nerves Of Cities)" (3:31) a slowed down PROCOL HARUM-like sound palette that comes off sounding like something from a Blues-Rock band like anything lead by vocalist ALEX LIGERTWOOD, Billy Gibbons, or 21st Century Polish band LIZARD. At the very end the band do a quick shift into high gear for minute of rousing organ-led instrumental fun to finish things off. (8.875/10)4. "Senne Wędr'wki (Wandering Dreams)" (3:52) orchestra-supported blues rock! Interesting! Quite like the sound of PROCOL HARUM. Nice imagination! (9/10)5. "Taniec Wariatki (The Madwoman's Dance)" (2:02) rock-infused theatric cabaret music (almost musique concr'te) with interesting call-and-response playfulness between the instrumentalists. Quite creative. (4.625/5)6. "Taniec Czterech (The Four Men's Dance)" (1:37) fun/funny open air, city green music by the local marching band. Nice drumming. (4.375/5)7. "Na Przek'r (Against Everything)" (2:16) opens like some folk rock from one of the Summer of Love's outdoor music festivals--with vocals (DON BREWER-like lead with Gospel church choir backing), like a. moralistic hippy musical. (4.625/5)8. "Nasze Myśli (Thoughts)" (5:10) pensive four chord progression arpeggiated by guitar with organ, drums, and bass backing while lead singer croons like a South American folk singer singing through the city center's public address system (or else LIZARD's Damian Bydliński). The very pleasant and comforting song contains a somewhat-spirited organ solo but is really just more of a nice ballad. Interesting vocal weave at the finish. Reminds me of 1990s QUIDAM. (9/10)9. "Mrowisko (The Hive)" (4:15) unusual opening with drums and organ playing cat-and-mouse-in-the-mirror for the first 35 seconds. Then a pause opens the door for a classical guitar and intermittent bombastic "symphonic" bursts of accompaniment and antiphonal response--something that gets drawn out for a minute, stumbling and fumbling, until finally fully developed at the three-minute mark. From there we get a minute of song with singing. Weird. (So like the 21st Century music of Polish band LIZARD). Yet interesting. And creative. (9/10)10. "Pejzaż Z Pustych Ram (Landscape Of Empty Frames)" (4:31) gentle electric guitar musings accompanied by responsive ghost-vocalese open this before a fully-meted song presents itself at 1:10. Singer Marek Alaszewski sounds like Jacques Brel during the delicate verse, but then things amp up for the chorus, Marek switching voice tones to something more RPI like as choir vocals chase him around like a church choir. Nice bass work from Roman Pawelski as the band and vocalists sustain the chorus intensity from here to the song's end. Very nice: emotional. (9/10)11. "Taniec Głodnego (The Starvelling's Dance)" (2:24) PROCOL HARUM palette and slow militaristic pace as organ swirls, drum and bass keep funereal time, and wooden flute (recorder) presents and carries the lead over the top. The opening motif switches into something more dance-oriented at 1:38 as Roman shifts to a walking bass line. Sounds like a wonderful night for a Moondance (Van Morrison)! Nice! (4.5/5)12. "Epidemia Euforii (Epidemic Euphory)" (3:46) not sure what is meant by this song's title, but the music feels more derivative of a combination of early British Rock and the U.S.'s Beatnik styles. By the time the band really kicks into full gear we're presented something that sounds more like Steve Winwood's first band, The Spencer Davis Group, as well as, at the percussion end, like The Chicago Transit Authority (with, of course, the Damian Bydliński lead vocal voice). (8.875/10)13. "Sen (A Dream)" (1:49) all four members of the rock combo are here represented with Marek dusting off his recorder again to muse over the gentle/calming nature-backed music. (4.375/5)Total time 41:59A very creative band of proficient musicians who create an unusual but very pleasing style of progressive rock: their songs are either isolated vignettes of imagination or conglomerations of such all smashed together. The bottom line is: that it works! I especially like the interesting use of choral backing vocals and full-spectrum and active percussion tracks.A-/4.5 stars; a collection of what feels like experimental and highly-idiosyncratic musical ideas coming from a very creative and skilled quartet of young musicians that results in a minor masterpiece of early progressive rock music. (There is little or no Jazz much less Jazz-Rock Fusion here).

items.body: Review by Finnforest — "After the Darkness, the Light" On their third and final album of the 1970s, Salis flipped the script once again, sounding nothinglike their previous effort five years prior. The Salis brothers were back, but they had a newdrummer and keyboardist in the lineup, and they obviously were hell-bent on forging a new direction.There is no sign of the debut's personality or the acoustic mellow vibe of the second. Here the bandhas shifted to that largely instrumental spacey fusion sound so common in the late '70s. The first reference that jumped into my mind was PFM's "Jet Lag" album, and I wondered if that wasan influence for Salis here, though "Jet Lag" is more adventurous than this. The mix of polishedrhythm section and quirky keyboard parts also reminded me just a bit of some of the instrumentalinterludes on later Cat Stevens albums. Another band this reminds me of is Finch. If you were intothem, you should enjoy these competent but sometimes tedious instrumentals. There are some very coollead guitar passages in several tracks. I suspect the approach is the reason why this album is ratedso much higher than their previous two, but frankly I don't see it. Yes, the longer jams overfloating keyboard atmosphere is going to appeal to progressive rock fans, but I think thecompositions on the first two albums are more interesting to me. Nevertheless, it is withoutquestion another good album by Salis. It all comes down to your tastes, naturally. I find this albumcompetent but pretty forgettable.

items._cn_summary: 这是意大利前卫摇滚乐队Salis的第三张也是最后一张专辑，发行于1979年。乐队在阵容上进行了调整，引入新鼓手与键盘手，风格从前两张作品的人物化气质与原声柔缓氛围彻底转向七十年代末常见的器乐主导、键盘氛围与融合爵士色彩的太空感声响。整张专辑以长段即兴展开为主，键盘铺设漂浮氛围层，吉他时有突出独奏段落穿插其中，节奏部处理较为精致。评论者将其与PFM的《Jet Lag》、Finch等乐队以及Cat Stevens器乐间奏相类比，认为演奏技术到位但部分段落略显冗长。整体而言，专辑在风格转型上展现出明确的方向性追求，器乐编排有可圈可点之处，但在深度与冒险性上未能超越乐队早期的作品。

items.body: Demonwarp released “Viral Empire” on Re:Mission Entertainment on 25 September 2026. The album is Demonwarp’s third full-length, running ten original tracks of industrial and EBM rhythm work layered with dark synth and metal-edged electronics, its lyrics turning on surveillance, corruption, artificial intelligence and resistance to power. Viral Empire by Demonwarp Two tracks were released as singles ahead of the album: “Protocol Obey” and “Spreading The Flames.” “Viral Empire” adds three remixes of those singles to close out its thirteen-track sequence: Frontal Boundary reworks “Protocol Obey,” while Dawn Of Ashes and Dread Risks each contribute separate versions of “Spreading The Flames.” Demonwarp handled all production and vocals on the album; Kristof Bathory mastered it, and KGM Studio supplied the cover art. Pre-orders opened on 4 September ahead of the 25 September release. The first pressing is a limited run of 100 digipak CDs, alongside the full digital release on Bandcamp. “Viral Empire” follows 2024’s “Dominion,” Demonwarp’s second album, which featured Jenna Cogan on vocals. About Demonwarp Demonwarp began self-releasing music in 2022 with the single “Devil’s Sunset” and the ten-track album “In The Night,” followed the same year by the singles “Relent” and “Lust Lies In Betrayal.” Further self-released singles, “Just Ashes,” “Scream At The Gates,” “Onikiri” and “Fading Flesh,” followed through 2023. Demonwarp’s second album, “Dominion,” arrived in September 2024 with Jenna Cogan featured on vocals. “Viral Empire,” Demonwarp’s third full-length, arrived on 25 September 2026 through Re:Mission Entertainment, preceded by the singles “Protocol Obey” and “Spreading The Flames” and the remixes of both that close the new album.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Demonwarp的第三张全长作品，包含十首原创曲目及三首混音版本，总共十三首。音乐以工业与EBM节奏结构为骨架，叠加暗潮合成器音色与金属质感的电子音效。歌词主题围绕监控、权力腐败、人工智能与反抗展开，具有明显的赛博朋克式批判视角。制作方面，由艺术家本人独立完成所有编曲与人声录制，Kristof Bathory负责母带处理，KGM Studio提供封面设计。发行形式为限量100张的Digipak CD及Bandcamp数字版，由小厂牌Re:Mission Entertainment发行。整体制作属于工业/EBM体系内的标准范式，主题与声音美学统一，但在声音设计的实验性和突破性方面缺乏更深入的探索。
